items.descriptionOriginal: Nearly every parent hopes their child will be better off than they are: smarter, more secure, and more well-adjusted. Many parents see this as a stamp of successful parenting, but something has changed for children growing up today. While younger generations are known for their empathy , one neuroscientist argues their cognitive capabilities are lagging behind those of previous generations, a claim that remains debated. Dr. Jared Cooney Horvath, a teacher turned cognitive neuroscientist who focuses on human learning, testified before the U.S. Senate Commerce Committee in January 2026 about concerns over cognitive development in children . In his testimony, he said, “A sad fact that our generation has to face is this: our kids are less cognitively capable than we were at their age. Since we’ve been standardizing and measuring cognitive development since the late 1800s, every generation has outperformed their parents, and that’s exactly what we want. We want sharper kids.” Student smiling in a classroom, working on a laptop. Photo credit: Canva So what’s actually causing the decline? Horvath explains that the reason this happens is that each generation has gone to school longer than the previous generation. Gen Z is no exception to the longer duration of time spent in school, but, according to Horvath, they’re the first ones who aren’t meeting this normal increase in cognitive development. The cognitive neuroscientist links the decline to the widespread introduction of screens in the classroom, which started around 2010. “Across 80 countries, if you look at the data, once countries adopt digital technology widely in schools , performance goes down significantly. To the point where kids who use computers about five hours per day in school for learning purposes will score over two-thirds of a standard deviation less than kids who rarely or never touch tech at school,” Horvath reveals. In most cases, the decline in performance doesn’t result in better strategies. The neuroscientist shares that the standardized testing has been adjusted to accommodate lower expectations and shorter attention spans. This is an approach that educators, scientists, and researchers went to Capitol Hill to express wasn’t working. But not every country is taking the approach of lowering standards to meet lowered cognitive ability. Denmark went in the opposite direction when it realized its students were slipping behind. Denmark decided to do something about it France24 interviewed educators in Denmark following its seemingly novel approach to students struggling with cognitive development. Since the beginning of the 2025/2026 school year, Denmark has not only been having students turn in their cellphones , but they’ve also invested heavily in physical books and scaled back digital learning. Danes went old school by bringing back physical textbooks , workbooks, and writing assignments. Early reactions have been positive, and even some students say they appreciate the countrywide shift in educational approach. “I think the biggest issue has been that, because we kind of got rid of the books and started using screens instead, that we’ve noticed that a lot of the kids have trouble concentrating, so it’s pretty easy to swipe with three fingers over to a different screen and have a video game going, for example, in class,” Copenhagen English teacher Islam Dijab told France 24. Now, instead of computers being part of every lesson, Danish schools are using computers more sparingly and with more supervision. One student says that it has been nice not having screen time at school because she loves to read and write. But it wasn’t just a lack of attention span. Children were also developing low self-esteem and poor mental health due to the amount of time spent on devices. And the effort goes beyond the classroom Concerns about the impact of screens on teens’ brains have prompted a nationwide change in Denmark that extends outside of the classroom. Afterschool activities are eliminating or extremely limiting electronic use. There is also a national No Phone Day that encourages everyone to put away their devices for the day, and Imran Rashid, a physician and digital health expert, has pushed for a ban on social media use for children under 15. In November 2025, the Danish government agreed to a plan to do just that, and a draft bill is now expected to take effect in July 2027 if parliament passes it. The no-phone movement in Denmark is a nationwide effort that hopes to right the ship before another generation feels the effects. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post Gen Z is the first generation less cognitively capable than their parents but Denmark has a solution appeared first on Upworthy .

items.title: Ο Αμερικανός μοιράζεται τις 9 συνειδητοποιήσεις του για τις ΗΠΑ μετά από 13 χρόνια στο εξωτερικό και είναι εντυπωσιακά

Σκέφτηκε τον χρόνο του στο Λονδίνο ως μια «προσωρινή περιπέτεια». Όταν όμως τελείωσε το πτυχίο του, βρέθηκε σε ένα απρόσμενο…
items.descriptionOriginal: Evan Edinger moved to London over a decade ago to study abroad but never planned on staying overseas permanently. His goal was to get his degree, return to the United States , start his career, and make a life for himself. He thought of his time in London as a “temporary adventure.” But when he finished his degree, he found himself in an unexpected situation: He didn’t want to go back. “The longer I stayed in London,” Edinger shares on his YouTube channel, “the more I began to notice all of the assumptions that I’d grown up believing in America, the things I was brought up to believe were undeniably true and just the way the world worked. It turns out they weren’t true at all.” One of the benefits of living in another country is seeing your country of origin through different eyes. That perspective can cause you to appreciate some things and question other things. Edinger shares nine realizations he’s had about the U.S. since he left, starting with one of the most quintessentially American realities he found himself questioning. Starting with the hardest one: guns 1. Guns Edinger grew up in New Jersey and describes it as “quite a blue state,” but he was still immersed in the gun culture that views gun ownership as a fundamental part of being an American. “I was raised in a very pro-gun household,” Edinger says. “In my family home in America, we had a 12-gauge shotgun, a 10-gauge, a black powder rifle, and a .410 shotgun for the children. My dad would take us out some days to shoot empty cans of beer or clay pigeons or sometimes go hunting for pheasants or deer.” He says the notion of not owning a gun was unthinkable in his upbringing. “The idea that other countries do not allow guns is viewed more like these other countries are missing a fundamental right,” he says. His ideas about guns have changed dramatically since moving to London and living in a society without ubiquitous access to guns. “Visiting Philadelphia when I was younger was always scary to me because I never knew who had a gun, who wanted to rob me,” Edinger shares. “Visiting New Orleans a couple years ago, I was told by my hotel staff that a few days prior, a tourist was shot and died in the local Popeye’s Chicken because he caught a stray bullet of two people having an argument in the restaurant. So, that’s just something that people just have to deal with. This constant fear of I could just die being caught in a crossfire and there’s nothing I can really do about it because freedom. I’ve pretty much never felt that level of fear in London at all. And that alone was enough to sway my opinion on guns.” 2. Government “One thing that’s really drilled into you pretty much every year of American school is that American democracy is the end-all be-all of government and that it is the beacon of freedom other countries look to emulate. Then, once you become an adult and you see how dysfunctional the U.S. government is, you search for anything to feel better about it and usually settle on ‘Well, at least it’s not a third world dictatorship.'” But those aren’t the only two options. Edinger explains how the parliamentary system in the U.K. is far from perfect, but it tends to be more effective at actually getting things done because lawmakers aren’t constantly stymied by the inherently destructive two-party gridlock we have in the U.S. “It’s messy, yes, but after 13 years away, I’ve come to the belief that no system of government is perfect,” he says. “But most systems in Western Europe are far more effective than what I grew up believing was the ‘best in the world.'” 3. Walkability and Public Transport Mass transit has its perks. Photo credit: Canva In the U.S., having a car is practically a symbol of freedom, but Edinger says he’s never felt the need to have a car in all his years living in London. He says it’s been incredibly freeing to be able to walk and take public transit everywhere, and not just in the city. He’s been able to travel all over Europe, in larger cities and small towns, and the focus on walkable neighborhoods and public transportation is everywhere. “After having spent some time living in walkable neighborhoods, I would never ever choose to live in a car dependent place ever again,” Edinger says. “It is truly one of the most life-changing parts of living over here. And because I’m always walking everywhere, because I’m always cycling everywhere, it’s so much easier to be healthy and physically fit without even trying.” 4. Food Quality and Price Europe has different regulations than the U.S., Edinger explains, with an approach that leads to a lot fewer additives and chemicals being added to foods. “ Europe’s food agency focuses on possibilities and the U.S.’s focuses on probabilities . Is it possible an unnecessary additive could be harmful? Europe prohibits it just to be safe. The U.S. agency, the FDA, they only step in if the probability of it being harmful is high. So, that risk is passed on to the average American consumer.” Edinger also points out that the ability to walk down to the store to get fresh ingredients regularly makes it a lot easier to eat well. “It’s one of those things where once you experience both, there is no contest. No contest. So, it’s much easier to be healthy in Europe than in America.” The social safety net ones hit hardest 5. Healthcare in the U.S. vs. Europe “If my health does have issues, I am glad it’s not something that would ever bankrupt me or cause me to ever think about how much it would have to cost me just to be sick,” says Edinger. Americans often hear horror stories about socialized medicine , but Edinger’s experience with going to the doctor and even going to the hospital has been positive, and barely cost him anything. “There are only two types of people that are against the freeing social safety net that is universal healthcare,” says Edinger. “People that have never experienced socialized healthcare and people that profit from the broken system. That’s it.” Most Americans want it, but “most Americans” is not where the money is. 6. Consumer Protections in the U.S. vs Europe Edinger shares that he bought a MacBook Pro in 2019 that didn’t work right, and he hadn’t purchased AppleCare because he knew he didn’t have to. “If you buy a tech product in Europe, you have a reasonable expectation that it should last you at least two years free of defects,” says Edinger. “And if it’s not up to your expectations or breaks down before then, you can demand a return or replacement. This law protects consumers from shady business practices.” He ended up getting his full money back on the computer due to those consumer protections. “It’s laws like this where you really begin to notice a pattern that life in Europe is one that gives more rights to the everyday person over giant corporations and shared benefit over private,” says Edinger. 7. Worker Rights “A quick summary would be 28 days minimum paid holiday, one year paid maternity leave, two weeks paid paternity leave, sick leave, even the right against unlawful termination,” said Edinger. “When working part-time at Urban Outfitters in London, even though I worked less than 20 hours a week, I still got two days paid holiday per month. That’s insane, right? No, that’s just life over here. Meanwhile, I worked five years at a Pizza Hut in New Jersey for over 30 hours per week. Never got a single day of paid vacation.” Indeed, there’s more than a handful of European countries that guarantee at least a month of paid days off, with some countries actually requiring a certain number of days or weeks off. Europeans get far more generous paid leave than Americans do. Photo credit: Canva Edinger points out the irony that he was always taught that the U.S. was for the individual, for individual freedoms. But in his experience, in Europe individuals have more rights than those with money or power, while it’s the opposite in the U.S. 8. Money (Live to work or work to live?) Edinger says that most things are more affordable in Europe, from groceries to data plans, but Americans do earn higher salaries . “So if you earn a lot of money and money is your sole defining metric of success, then you can feel a lot more successful in the U.S.,” he says. “But because the culture in Europe is work to live and not live to work, you might find that the stress and cost tradeoffs and quality of life erode the value of that higher salary quite quickly.” What does he actually miss about America? 9. On Romanticizing Europe People often wonder if Americans romanticize Europe too much, and Edinger says the same question used to be asked of Europeans romanticizing America. But now that we have YouTube and social media and a better ability to see the realities of both places, he says what Americans “romanticize” about Europe is really just the things we want and don’t have. “I think most Americans who are eyeing up Europe are doing so because of the things that America is lacking. Nearly two in three Americans want universal healthcare. Well, America doesn’t offer that. Again, two in three Americans want European style vacation policies. America doesn’t offer that. And 53% of Americans would prefer to live in a walkable neighborhood , but sorry, America doesn’t offer that. The list goes on. If America were an actual democracy, I don’t think many of these people would be having romanticized views of Europe at all because they wouldn’t need to. They could have everything they wanted in the country they were born and raised.” Every place has tradeoffs, he admits Of course, every country has its problems and there are certainly downsides to moving abroad. Edinger acknowledges that but says it really boils down to what you value in life. Americans are taught to romanticize the U.S., and leaving it helps you see the reality, what’s good about your country and where it has room for improvement. “I think the main thing though out of everything that I miss about the U.S. that I can’t really get here is not rights, not freedoms, not anything that’s big on quality of life improvements,” says Edinger. “It’s just Mexican food and good ice cream.” You can follow Evan Edinger on YouTube for more on his experiences as an American living abroad. This article originally appeared last year. It has been updated. The post American shares his 9 realizations about the U.S. after 13 years abroad and it’s eye-opening appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: Watching a game show from the comfort of home is easy. Being on one is a totally different ball game. The lights, the cameras, the pressure. It’s enough to make anyone’s brain freeze up. And is there any game show that allows contestants to royally embarrass themselves on national TV quite like Wheel of Fortune ? There’s always someone going viral for taking a big swing and missing on a phrase that seemed pretty apparent to the casual viewer. And when you take a big loss on a WOF word puzzle, there are a lot of folks shaking their heads at home. More than 8 million people watch the game show every night. Yikes. One rather notorious victim of the wheel was Gishma Tabari from Encino, California, whose fantasy-inspired whiff of a common phrase in December 2023 earned her a lot of groans and some support from those who thought her imagination was inspiring. The 3-word puzzle read: “TH _ _ RITI _ S _ GR _ E,” and Tabari offered the answer, “The British Ogre.” The guess surprised then-host Pat Sajak, who responded, “Uh, no.” Tabari must have missed that there was a space between the R and the E in the puzzle, so ogre would have had to be spelled with 2 Rs. She also probably wasn’t aware that England isn’t a place known for its ogres. The correct answer was: “The Critics Agree.” The British Ogre. Umm? #WheelOfFortune #TheBritishOgre pic.twitter.com/VnYcl0p7nE — Rick (@Rick_LifeCoach) December 13, 2023 A Wheel of Fortune instant classic The answer inspired a lot of activity on X, where people couldn’t believe someone could come up with such a fanciful answer to a puzzle with such a straightforward solution. This woman just guessed this puzzle as The British Ogre dying laughing so many British Ogres in show biz #WheelofFortune pic.twitter.com/2ooImWepDn — CoL* (@littleruk) December 13, 2023 This girl guessed “The British Ogre” on wheel of fortune and the second hand embarrassment was overwhelming. She wouldn’t even look at the camera for a sec I feel bad but man that shit was funny — Thumser (@JeffreyThumser) December 13, 2023 One person even created a lovely image of what could be the British Ogre. #WheelofFortune https://t.co/uNaDdAttl2 pic.twitter.com/sXJgeOfQPL — Michael Nge (@michaelnge283) December 13, 2023 Although… not everyone had a problem with the guess. The British Ogre sounds like a cool band name. #WheelofFortune — ᴊᴇʀᴇᴍʏ ᴊᴀᴍᴍ (@NaskarrKid) December 13, 2023 Where ogres actually come from On the bright side, the incorrect guess is an opportunity for the world to learn that ogres aren’t a significant part of English folklore. Sure, there are creatures in English literature and folklore with ogre-like qualities, such as Grendel from the Old English poem “Beowulf,” the monster that terrorizes the mead hall of King Hrothgar. There’s also the Boggart, a mischievous spirit much like a hobgoblin, and trolls, which appear in some English tales although they originate in Scandinavia. If you’re looking for ogres in Europe, France is the best place to go. The word ogre is of French descent and comes from the name of the Etruscan god of the underworld, Orcus. Orcus is a large, ugly, bearded giant who enjoys consuming human flesh. Ogres are primarily known for eating children, which they believe will give them eternal life. A new era for Wheel of Fortune As for Wheel of Fortune, the show has continued to evolve since. Pat Sajak stepped down after hosting for 41 years, with his final episode airing June 7, 2024. Ryan Seacrest, the longtime “American Idol” host, took over hosting duties that September, and has since hosted two full seasons alongside co-host Vanna White. In March 2026, the show was renewed for two more seasons, taking it through 2027, though White’s own contract, extended through the 2025-2026 season, hadn’t yet been confirmed to continue at the time of the renewal announcement. Sajak, for his part, has made the occasional return trip, including a guest appearance on Celebrity Wheel of Fortune, performing what he called his “ Final Spin .” And in case you’re wondering how Tabari is doing: on her Instagram she wears her “Wheel of Fortune Flub Girl” title with pride, declaring she is “British Ogre for life.” This article originally appeared three years ago. It has been updated. The post Woman’s whimsical ‘Wheel of Fortune’ guess is so bad it made her an instant legend appeared first on Upworthy .

items.descriptionOriginal: In Kerala, your father’s property could belong to your aunt’s children! Just like in the new series AKKA, for centuries, many Nair families followed a unique matrilineal system called Marumakkathayam, where family identity and inheritance passed through the mother’s side. Even a king’s son could not inherit the throne. It went to his sister’s son! But here’s the twist: women passed down the family name, while men, especially the eldest maternal uncle, held the power. The system was abolished in 1975, but matrilineal traditions continue in parts of India. items.descriptionOriginal: In Bajaura, in Himachal Pradesh's Kullu district, farmers have had to rethink their orchards twice. As changing weather made apple cultivation harder, they turned to pomegranates. Then plant viruses began affecting those orchards too. Now, persimmons are offering another possibility. For anyone who associates Himachal with bags of apples brought home after a holiday, that change may be surprising. For the people tending these orchards, it comes down to a pressing question: what can they grow to keep earning from their land? Rising temperatures, declining snowfall and unpredictable rainfall are making familiar crops harder to rely on. Farmers are responding by trying different fruits, growing crops together and changing how they care for their soil. Their efforts feature in a study by the Council on Energy, Environment and Water (CEEW), supported by the International Centre for Integrated Mountain Development (ICIMOD). Released on 31 October 2026, it draws on experiences across 12 gram panchayats in Mandi, Kullu, Sirmaur and Shimla . The study identifies 25 ways communities can prepare for climate risks. Among them are practices villagers have already begun putting to work, shaped by what they see happening in their fields and around their homes. What do you plant when the familiar crop struggles? Bajaura's move towards persimmons shows how much adjustment farming now demands. Replacing apples with pomegranates did not end the uncertainty. Farmers had to look for another option when disease affected the replacement crop. Growing a mix of crops can help spread the risk of a poor harvest, though poor transport and limited cold storage still constrain farmers' earnings. Photograph: (Himachal Watcher) And choosing a fruit is only part of making an orchard viable. Farmers need water to grow it and roads to get the harvest to buyers. In Bajaura, dwindling irrigation water and roads damaged during disasters continue to make both difficult. In Parara, Sirmaur, growers face a related problem. Residents report that changing rainfall and rising temperatures have altered planting schedules and increased diseases affecting tomatoes and garlic. Some farmers are combining garlic cultivation with specialised apple varieties . The village's efforts also include natural farming and rainwater harvesting. Growing a mix of crops can help spread the risk of a poor harvest, though poor transport and limited cold storage still constrain farmers' earnings. For a farming household, finding something that grows is the beginning. Being able to sell it is what helps pay the bills. In Sandhu, change begins with the soil In Sandhu, Shimla, farmers are reconsidering how they grow their crops. Community members report that prolonged chemical fertiliser use has affected soil quality and fertility. Local women have responded by taking up natural farming, which avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides and uses resources available on the farm. The aim is to nurture the soil while reducing reliance on purchased chemical inputs . According to community accounts documented in the study, the practice has spread to more than 20 families after residents found it profitable and better able to withstand extreme weather. That experience gives neighbours something practical to consider: a different way of farming already being tried close to home. Yet even healthier soil and a different crop need water. In nearby Sirmaur district, that has brought women's groups back to the traditional sources their villages once relied on. Bringing water back to village life Thana Kashoga once had 35 perennial baoris, traditional spring-fed water structures that supplied households throughout the year. According to the study, only 10 remain. Residents report declining rainfall and rising temperatures , putting increasing pressure on these sources. The shortage reaches into everyday life, affecting drinking water, irrigation and livestock. Fodder scarcity and forest fires have also made pastoral livelihoods harder to sustain. Local women have responded by taking up natural farming, which avoids synthetic fertilisers and pesticides and uses resources available on the farm. The aim is to nurture the soil while reducing reliance on purchased chemical inputs. Photograph: (Triya Gulati via The Print) Women's groups have taken on the work of maintaining and restoring the baoris. Their efforts connect directly to what farmers are trying to do: keep village life possible as the conditions supporting it change. These communities still need dependable irrigation, transport and support to carry their work forward. A new crop cannot fix a damaged road, and a restored water source needs continued care. But in Thana Kashoga, there is a tangible reason to keep going. Women's groups clean the baoris monthly. Five springs have been revived, with work on another five or six under way. Sources: 'Villages in Himachal adapting climate change with new crops, revived springs' : By Shailee Dogra, Published on 1 November 2026 'How can Himalayan communities anticipate risks and adapt to a changing climate? Evidence from 12 Gram Panchayats of Himachal Pradesh' : By Ahana Chatterjee, Meet Kumar, Srishti Mandal, Taveri Rajkhowa, and Shreya Wadhawan, Published on 31 October, 2026

Τέσσερις μήνες αφότου η κόρη της μετακόμισε σε ένα νέο σχολείο, η Shivani Tyagi αποφάσισε να ξαναδείτε την εμπειρία της με ένα…
items.descriptionOriginal: For a five-year-old, changing schools can mean more than walking into a new classroom or learning a different routine. It can also mean leaving behind familiar faces, favourite teachers and friends who have been part of their everyday lives. Four months after her daughter moved to a new school, Shivani Tyagi decided to revisit the experience with a simple question: "When we changed your school, how did you feel?" Her daughter's answer caught her attention. "It was very upsetting," she said, explaining that the hardest part was leaving her friends behind. She hadn't wanted to do that. Even after settling into a new school, children may need time and space to process the emotions of leaving old friends behind. Rather than brushing aside the response or reassuring her that everything was fine, Shivani chose to listen and ask her daughter more about how she had managed the change. Making room for difficult feelings Shivani, a certified nutritionist, parent coach and NLP coach, believes that children do not always express what they are feeling immediately. Sometimes, they need time, reassurance and a comfortable space to put their emotions into words. Her daughter had settled into the new school, made friends and appeared to be adjusting well. But Shivani wanted to understand what the transition had felt like from her daughter's perspective. When she asked how she had managed the move despite finding it upsetting, her daughter explained that she was willing to try. Having the space to express what she was feeling made it easier for her to navigate the change. View this post on Instagram A post shared by Shivani Tyagi - Parent coach, Nutritionist, NLP practitioner (@parenting_with_shivani) For Shivani, that was a moment of pride. She was happy to see her daughter acknowledge that something had been difficult while still finding the courage to give a new environment a chance. She also understood that making new friends did not mean forgetting the old ones. They could still stay in touch with their previous classmates while gradually building new friendships. Keep asking, even after they seem settled School transitions can bring a mix of emotions for young children. Excitement about a new classroom may exist alongside sadness about leaving familiar surroundings. And just because a child appears comfortable after a few weeks does not necessarily mean they have processed everything. This is why Shivani makes it a habit to have open conversations with her daughter about everyday experiences, whether big or small. For parents navigating a similar transition, the approach need not be complicated. A simple conversation over dinner, during a bedtime routine or on the way back from school can create an opportunity for children to share what is on their minds. Simple everyday conversations can help children feel safe expressing emotions they may otherwise struggle to put into words. Instead of immediately offering solutions, parents can begin by asking what they miss, what they enjoy about the new school or whether anything has been difficult. The idea is not to have all the answers but to let children know that their feelings are welcome. Sometimes, a child does not need to be told that everything will be fine. They simply need to know that they can talk about what isn't. All images courtesy of Shivani Tyagi Source: 'Helping Kids Handle Change at School' by PBS Kids, Published on 11 January 2022.

items.descriptionOriginal: In South Sudan in 2024, just out of high school, Nyakangba Nelson Luka Poyo asked himself what kind of life a kid born in 2021 in Tambura would have apart from killing, hatred, bloodshed, and living in a camp. Amid tears, that question gave him his life’s purpose. He thought if young people had opportunities to learn and communicate, and the space in which to express themselves, they could realize alternatives to violence. He called it a “Peace Voice.” Young people make up an estimated 70% of South Sudan’s population, yet they have no voice. They are swept up into conflict at a shockingly young age. In a Peace Journey program, Nyakangba learned about Laddership, and how to become a “ladder” for others lifting them up through support and opportunities. Now, through Peace Voices to Vision, he helps young people “develop a common understanding of how to live together peacefully. Everyone deserves peace.”

items.descriptionOriginal: This article is published in partnership with Museum of Solutions For a child who has never used a computer independently, the first lesson in artificial intelligence isn't about algorithms. It's about a cursor. For one Grade 6 student from a government school in Maharashtra's Raigad district, that lesson began inside a 10-storey children's museum in Mumbai's Lower Parel, tucked into the old Kamala Mills compound: the Museum of Solutions (MuSo). When the student joined an immersive artificial intelligence (AI) learning programme there, computers were still unfamiliar territory. Even using a laptop touchpad and typing basic commands were challenges. But over the next few sessions, that began to change. By the end of the programme, the student had created an email account, learnt to use Microsoft Word and OneDrive, and taken part in coding challenges through Minecraft Education. What started with the basics of operating a computer had opened a door to exploring artificial intelligence, experimenting with technology and understanding how it works. "From day one, it was pretty interesting. The AI workshop at the Museum of Solutions brought teachers and students together to learn about technology, explore AI and understand how it can be used to find solutions to different problems, from those in our classrooms to challenges at a global level," says Meera, a student, who attended the workshop at MuSo. For thousands of children from underserved communities across Maharashtra, such opportunities are becoming a first introduction to the technology that is increasingly shaping the world around them. Students experiment with machine learning by training models to recognise objects and understanding how the information they receive shapes their results. Through AI Explorers, an initiative at MuSo, children are learning about AI through interactive games, experiments, creative exercises and coding activities. The programme, supported by Microsoft Philanthropies India and implemented by JSW Foundation, aims to make AI education more accessible to children who may have limited opportunities to engage with digital learning. Between July 2025 and June 2026, the initiative reached 9,087 children through foundational AI workshops, while another 313 students took part in a more intensive 10-hour learning pilot. It also trained 80 teachers and worked with 36 schools and 17 NGO and community partners across six districts of Maharashtra. But the numbers tell only part of the story. At its heart, the initiative is about making sure that a child's access to emerging technologies is not decided by the circumstances they grow up in. Bringing AI education beyond privileged classrooms AI is already influencing how children interact with the world, from the content they watch to the apps they use. But knowing how to use a digital device and understanding the technology behind it are two very different things. For children from underserved communities, opportunities to explore AI, experiment with coding or even use a computer independently can be limited. The data bears this out. According to the Ministry of Education's UDISE+ 2024-25 data, only 57.9% of schools in India have computers that work for teaching, and in government schools the figure falls to 52.7%. In Maharashtra, more than 25,000 of the state's 1.08 lakh schools, nearly one in four, had no functional computer. Children explore how AI works through interactive activities, learning to question its outputs rather than simply accept them. At home, the gap is wider still. The ASER 2023 'Beyond Basics' survey of rural youth aged 14 to 18 found that while about 90% of households had a smartphone, only 9% had a computer or laptop. Those with a computer at home were far more likely to know how to use one (85%) than those without (33.9%). Meanwhile, AI is arriving in classrooms. From the 2026-27 academic year, the Ministry of Education is introducing AI and computational thinking in schools from Class 3 onwards. This gap led MuSo to conceptualise AI Explorers. It's a natural fit for a museum whose very name is a mission statement. Opened in November 2023 by the JSW Group and founded by Tanvi Jindal Shete, a former Teach For India fellow, the not-for-profit museum aims to empower children to find solutions to India's most pressing problems. Within a year, it was named on TIME's list of the World's Greatest Places of 2024 and became the first Indian museum to win the international Hands On! Children in Museums Award, competing against 32 museums from 17 countries. "AI already shapes children's lives through the phones in their homes, the apps they use and the content they are shown. Yet children from underserved communities rarely get the chance to understand how it works, let alone question it," says Susan Vaidyan, Head of Education MuSo. The programme introduces students from Classes 5 to 10 to foundational AI concepts, machine learning, prompt engineering, digital literacy, coding and responsible technology use. Rather than beginning with technical explanations, the sessions use familiar examples and hands-on activities. In one activity, students use a teachable machine to train a machine-learning model to recognise different objects or images. They experiment with the data being fed into the system, and then do something unexpected: they deliberately train it incorrectly to see what happens. When the model begins producing inaccurate results, the children grasp an important truth about AI: its outputs depend on the information it learns from. The programme also introduces students to AI-generated creativity, prompt-based exercises and community problem-solving challenges, allowing them to explore how the technology can be applied to everyday situations. Microsoft's involvement brings technology platforms, learning resources and expertise in responsible AI to the programme. The programme introduces children to responsible AI use, including online privacy, misinformation, bias and cyber safety. "An inclusive AI economy cannot begin at college or the workplace; it has to begin in the classroom," says Kishore Kumar Thangavelu, CSR Lead, Microsoft Corporation India Private Limited. Through Microsoft 365, students learn to create email accounts, organise their work using OneDrive, write documents in Word and use Excel to organise information. They also explore Copilot to improve sentences, summarise information and help with everyday tasks. Minecraft Education and MakeCode introduce coding through play. Students programme a virtual agent to chop trees, build walls and construct structures using instructions, loops and conditional statements. The programme also uses Minecraft's CyberSafe world to introduce online safety through games and practical challenges. That matters: ASER 2023 found that nearly half of rural young people on social media didn't know basic safety features, such as blocking or reporting a profile. But the learning isn't limited to how these tools work. Children are also encouraged to question the technology, recognise its limits and consider when it should or shouldn't be used. AI Explorers began as a two-hour introductory workshop. But the team soon realised that children needed more time to move beyond demonstrations and engage with the concepts themselves. "It's important for children to not just use AI tools but to question their outputs and understand their limitations," says Susan. The 10-hour programme, spread across three days, gives children the time to do just that. They begin by exploring how AI and machine learning work, including the exercise where they deliberately train a model with incorrect information. On the second day, they explore agentic AI through block coding and a game that shows how AI agents observe their surroundings and make decisions. The final day focuses on responsible AI, covering privacy, transparency and bias, with examples such as deepfakes, phishing and voice assistants that struggle with different accents. Coding activities through Minecraft Education help students understand instructions, loops and conditional statements while learning through play. For Susan, the aim is to move children beyond watching demonstrations to experimenting, asking questions and recognising that a machine's answers are not always right. "They stopped watching and started doing: trying things, getting wrong results and working out why," she says. Their questions began changing too, from what AI could do to how it arrived at an answer, and when its outputs should be questioned. What changes when children get access? Over the course of a year, AI Explorers reached 9,087 children through its foundational workshops. Another 313 students spent more time with the subject through the 10-hour immersive pilot. The programme travelled across six Maharashtra districts (Mumbai, Mumbai Suburban, Thane, Raigad, Ahilyanagar and Pune), reaching children through 36 government and aided schools and 17 NGO and community partners. There was also an effort to ensure girls were part of this learning experience. Of the 7,398 student records collected, 54% were girls. That matters in a country where, ASER 2023 found, rural boys were more than twice as likely as girls to own a smartphone, and half the boys surveyed had an email ID, compared with under 30% of girls. But what did the children take away from these sessions? Between July 2025 and June 2026, AI Explorers reached 9,087 children through foundational workshops across six districts of Maharashtra. The assessments offer some clues. In the foundational workshops, 81% of the students assessed showed greater interest in AI, while 61% showed an improvement in AI literacy. Among the 126 students assessed in the immersive pilot, 80% demonstrated an understanding of AI and machine learning. Around 75% showed awareness of coding and cyber safety, while the same proportion had set up an email ID and accessed Microsoft 365, in some cases for the first time. For some children, the change was also visible in how they began to look at technology. At a Marathi-medium school in Mumbai, a group of girls initially felt that technology and AI were too difficult for them. But as they experimented with AI games and prompt engineering, they began creating AI-generated content, discussing ethical questions and using digital tools to explore sustainability challenges. What had once seemed out of reach had become something they could try, question and create with. From first steps to future dreams The Raigad student's journey offers a glimpse of what this access can make possible. At the start of the immersive programme, using a touchpad and typing basic commands were challenges. By the end, the student had independently navigated several digital tools, created an email account and taken part in coding activities. For Meera, it was a fun, experience-oriented way of learning, where she learnt about AI in depth through games and interactive activities. For children with limited access to computers, the programme offers an opportunity to explore technology, build digital skills and imagine new possibilities. "What I found interesting was that we were not just learning about technology, but also understanding how to use it safely and think about things like online privacy, fake information and bias," she adds. As Susan puts it, success is not simply about children learning to use AI tools. It is about seeing them experiment, doubt what a machine tells them and ask questions of their own. As AI becomes part of more aspects of everyday life, the ability to question it may prove just as important as knowing how to use it. And that is a lesson these children are beginning to learn early. All images courtesy of Museum of Solutions team

items.descriptionOriginal: Every year, tonnes of paddy stubble are set on fire across Punjab, adding to the air pollution choking North India. But what if this farm waste could become something useful? For eight years, Gurdaspur-based innovator Parminder Singh experimented with paddy waste in his garage, even when people mocked his idea. His hard work led to an unusual innovation: drop-down ceiling tiles made using paddy stubble. Designed to provide heat and cold insulation, these tiles are also waterproof and fire-resistant. Through his startup, Agro Stubble Management, Parminder hopes to give farmers a reason to earn from crop residue instead of burning it. His vision is to establish production plants across Punjab, where discarded stubble can become a valuable raw material. It’s an idea that could turn agricultural waste into a resource, create livelihood opportunities and offer another way to tackle stubble burning. #StubbleBurning #Punjab #SustainableInnovation #ClimateAction #AgriTech

items.descriptionOriginal: For 560 children at New Life School in Dharavi, Mumbai, the future of their education depends on one question: will their school continue to exist where it stands today? The preschool has been educating children in the neighbourhood for four decades. Yet, throughout its 40-year history, it has never owned the land on which it operates. Now, as Dharavi undergoes redevelopment, securing that land has become central to ensuring the school's future. An effort to help the institution do so has brought together an unlikely group: a 19-year-old college student, his friends and a community determined to preserve access to education for the neighbourhood's children. Taking on a fundraising campaign of this scale meant Daniel had to understand several areas beyond his college curriculum, including corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, institutional philanthropy and campaign strategy. Daniel Gupta, a third-year advertising and media student at Mumbai University, is leading the effort through an initiative called Dharavi Rising. After raising Rs 22 lakh against an initial target of Rs 20 lakh for the school's expansion, the team has now set its sights on a much larger goal: Rs 1.5 crore to help the school secure its land and continue serving children in the neighbourhood. For Daniel, the initiative is about more than keeping a school open. It is also an attempt to change how people see Dharavi, a neighbourhood often discussed through the lens of overcrowding, poverty and redevelopment, rather than through the lives, aspirations and institutions of the people who call it home. And he is learning to take on this challenge while still attending college, without any prior fundraising experience or an established professional network. Building a movement around a school Daniel's connection with New Life School began through a friend whose parents run the institution. Learning about the school's four-decade-long journey also brought him face to face with a pressing question: how could an institution that had served generations of children secure a future for the next ones? "People are often surprised when they learn that this school has been running for 40 years without owning its land. We want more people to know that it exists and understand why securing its future matters," Daniel says. What began as an effort to support the school gradually took shape as Dharavi Rising, an initiative that brings together young people and the wider community to address the institution's long-standing challenges. For the teachers, the campaign offers an opportunity to draw attention to a school that has continued to serve children despite the uncertainty surrounding its future. "We wholeheartedly support Daniel's mission to secure the future of our school in Dharavi. We want to do everything we can to ensure that the children's education continues without disruption," say teachers Kelsi Rani Raja and D. Packia Hincy. For the teachers, the campaign offers an opportunity to draw attention to a school that has continued to serve children despite the uncertainty surrounding its future. Their support also reflects a practical concern for families who depend on accessible schooling. The team wants to preserve an institution that parents can afford, rather than see its future compromised by the changes taking place around it. From Rs 20 lakh to Rs 1.5 crore When Daniel and his college friends began working on Dharavi Rising in November 2025, the idea was to find creative ways for young people to contribute to a cause. Daniel was just 19 when he took on the responsibility of building the initiative. With no previous experience in fundraising or social-impact work , he had to learn how to approach potential donors, understand funding mechanisms and communicate the school's needs. The team's first fundraising effort set a target of Rs 20 lakh for the school's expansion. They eventually raised Rs 22 lakh, marking an important milestone for a student-led initiative. However, the initial achievement was only a starting point. The larger challenge of securing the land on which the school stands remained. View this post on Instagram A post shared by New Life School | Dharavi Rising (@new_life_school_dharavi) This prompted the team to launch Dharavi Rising 1.5, with a fundraising target of Rs 1.5 crore to help secure the school's future. The new campaign takes on a more ambitious, long-term challenge: ensuring that an institution that has educated generations of children can continue to do so. Learning to navigate an unfamiliar challenge Taking on a fundraising campaign of this scale meant Daniel had to understand several areas beyond his college curriculum, including corporate social responsibility (CSR) funding, institutional philanthropy and campaign strategy. "I had absolutely no prior experience in any of this, so I needed guidance. I realised there would genuinely be no better tool than ChatGPT," he says. Daniel had been using the AI tool even before starting Dharavi Rising. Like many students, he initially turned to it for help with college presentations and assignments. But as the initiative took shape, his questions became more specific. How does CSR funding work? What policies should he understand? How could he explain the initiative to potential supporters? What would a fundraising campaign need to communicate to people who knew little about the school? ChatGPT became one of the tools he used to work through these questions. "I used it to explore naming and branding ideas, work on campaign strategy , understand broad fundraising and CSR concepts, and develop outreach material. I also used it to identify website requirements and organise my thinking about how to present Dharavi Rising to prospective donors," he tells The Better India . The tool helped him break down an unfamiliar and complex task into smaller, more manageable steps. He also used AI-generated text in donor communications. View this post on Instagram A post shared by New Life School | Dharavi Rising (@new_life_school_dharavi) Daniel estimates that ChatGPT saves him two to three hours a day, helping him balance college with the demands of organising the campaign and communicating with potential donors. However, he recognises that AI cannot replace the judgement and effort required to run an initiative of this nature. He says he rejects suggestions that do not align with Dharavi Rising's objectives and is careful about the information he shares with the tool. He also acknowledges that he has not followed a systematic process to independently verify all the guidance generated by ChatGPT. Ultimately, the campaign continues to depend on people: the school staff who understand its needs, the families whose children attend it, the friends supporting the initiative and the donors willing to contribute. Keeping education within reach For New Life School's teachers, the central concern remains the children. The campaign is not simply about raising money for a building or an expansion. It is about helping secure the future of an educational institution that has remained accessible to families in the neighbourhood for four decades. The challenge now is to build on the team's initial achievement and reach enough people to support the school's longer-term needs. The challenge now is to build on that initial achievement and reach enough people to support the school's longer-term needs. For Daniel, the effort also carries a larger purpose: changing perceptions of Dharavi and highlighting the aspirations, initiatives and community institutions that exist within the neighbourhood. "My work with Dharavi Rising began with a desire to change perceptions of a neighbourhood. It has since developed into a concrete effort to help protect one of its educational institutions . Yes, AI has helped me navigate some of that unfamiliar territory, but the purpose of all our work remains rooted in the school and the children it serves," Daniel says, pointing at the colourful artwork-laden boards in the classroom where he was sitting during a conversation with The Better India . For the 560 children who attend New Life School, the goal is simple: to ensure that a school that has been part of their neighbourhood for decades can continue to be part of their future. This Children's Day, those who wish to support Daniel's efforts to secure the future of New Life School and its 560 children can contribute by visiting dharavirising.com and making a donation.

items.description: Η νόσος Lafora είναι μια σπάνια γενετική πάθηση που συνήθως επηρεάζει παιδιά και εφήβους, προκαλώντας συχνές κρίσεις και σταδιακή απώλεια της γνωστικής λειτουργίας. Δεν υπάρχει θεραπεία, επομένως η εστίαση για πολλούς γονείς αναπόφευκτα στρέφεται στην ποιότητα ζωής. Αυτό είναι κάτι που η μαμά του Ντιτρόιτ η Azeza Kasham πάλευε να διατηρήσει για τον 17χρονο γιο της, Gigi Breadiy.…
items.descriptionOriginal: Lafora disease is a rare genetic condition that typically affects kids and adolescents, causing frequent seizures and the gradual loss of cognitive function. There is no cure, so the focus for many parents inevitably turns to quality of life. That’s something Detroit mom Azeza Kasham was struggling to maintain for her 17-year-old son, Gigi Breadiy, earlier this year. He was diagnosed in 2019, just days after his older brother died of the disease. Kasham’s husband has his own health problems and isn’t able to work, and the couple has two younger boys as well, so she took on multiple jobs to pay off medical debt. Breadiy uses a wheelchair, and the family home wasn’t fully accessible, so caring for him was becoming increasingly difficult. She’d tried fundraising on social media, but still felt like she was drowning. A stranger she connected with online would be her rescue buoy. Josh Liljenquist is a Minnesota content creator with over 23 million followers. Many of his videos fall into the somewhat controversial random-acts-of-kindness genre, but the 28-year-old’s main focus is rallying tangible support for people in need. After learning about Breadiy, he posted footage of himself meeting mother and son in February. Less than two months later, a GoFundMe he launched for them had raised nearly $600,000. “It’s just completely changed my life, you know?” Kasham shared during a recent phone call with Nice News. “It’s enabled me to give Gigi everything he needs, but that’s not all [Josh] did. And that isn’t even the most important thing. He restored my faith in humanity.” In the nearly seven months since meeting, Liljenquist and Kasham have become extremely close. “She’s literally like my second mom,” he said, adding: “She keeps saying that I changed her life, but I think she changed my life more than I changed hers.” His own mother also speaks to her often, and even flew out to Michigan to spend time with the family. The women connected so strongly because they both know what it’s like to care for a sick child, and the financial toll it can take. For the first six years of Liljenquist’s life, he was in and out of the hospital. He has a genetic disorder called alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency as well as eosinophilic esophagitis, a chronic inflammatory disease of the esophagus. That background has led him to direct more energy into helping families experiencing similar situations. “I want other parents to not have to deal with the same thing that my parents dealt with,” he said. But his fundraising has benefited people in all sorts of circumstances: a man in need of a new roof, a couple facing homelessness, a woman hoping to open a permanent pay-what-you-can cafe. For Kasham, the support from Liljenquist’s felt like God had answered her prayers. He, too, felt a divine hand in their meeting. The fact that they belong to different religions was a moot point. “She kept asking me, ‘Well, you know, you’re a Christian person. I’m Muslim. Does that matter?’ And I’m like, ‘Oh my gosh, no, not at all,’” he recounted. “That’s the first thing she would ask me. And I said, ‘Why would that matter?’” Before the GoFundMe, Kasham had to bathe Breadiy in the garage because the shower wasn’t accessible. Now, the family has paid down debt and made upgrades to their home, including a roll-in shower, that allow him dignity and privacy. “He has his good days. He has his bad days,” she said, noting that his seizures have worsened in recent months. “But one thing he has that puts the biggest smile on his face is he has his own space.” You can donate to Lafora disease research through Chelsea’s Hope .

items.descriptionOriginal: Let the best of Anthropocene come to you. Sign up for our free newsletters Success! Email Newsletters Newsletters Science Dispatch (weekly) Fixing Carbon (twice a month) Sign up 5 Fixes for Low Carbon Buildings We spend most of our lives inside buildings, and the planet pays for it. Constructing and running the places where we live, work and learn accounts for about 27% of global emissions and nearly half of all the materials humans extract from the Earth. Half of the buildings that will be standing in 2050 still haven’t been built or renovated, which makes this a rare chance to get things right from the ground up. Here are five fixes that are reimagining how we design, build, heat and cool the spaces we live in. This concrete could turn your house into a battery The amount of concrete that goes into an average American home’s basement wall could hold enough energy to meet the daily needs of the household. Greener Steel Through Chemistry In a lab outside Boulder Colorado, engineers are reinventing one of the dirtiest industrial processes on Earth—by swapping fire for modern alchemy. These new building materials are alive, photosynthetic— and carbon hungry Scientists have engineered a living, carbon-capturing material that can be shaped by 3D printing and hardened over time through biological growth. This ‘living paint’ traps carbon dioxide and produces oxygen By encasing bacteria in a tough but porous coating, researchers have made paint that could be used to capture carbon and produce biofuels Wood, now turbocharged with carbon-capture powers Researchers created a novel wood composite that contains CO2-absorbing materials, paving the way for carbon-negative furniture and structures. items.title: Το CRISPR Enhancer Editing σώζει τα οργανοειδή του εγκεφάλου από τον αυτισμό
items.titleOriginal: CRISPR Enhancer Editing Rescues Autism Brain Organoids
items.description: Αντί να κόψουν το DNA, οι επιστήμονες χρησιμοποίησαν ακριβή ενεργοποίηση CRISPR με στόχο φυσικά γονιδιακά πλήκτρα για να ενισχύσουν υγιή αντίγραφα των CHD8 και SCN2A σε οργανοειδή ανθρώπινου εγκεφάλου, αποκαθιστώντας τη φυσιολογική ανάπτυξη των ιστών και την πυροδότηση νευρώνων αποκλειστικά σε μεταλλαγμένα κύτταρα.
items.descriptionOriginal: Rather than cutting DNA, scientists used precision CRISPR activation aimed at natural gene "dials" to boost healthy copies of CHD8 and SCN2A in human brain organoids, restoring normal tissue growth and neuronal firing exclusively in mutated cells.
