items.descriptionOriginal: Episode Description: Los Angeles tried to ban oil drilling once before, in 2022, and the oil companies won in court. This time, neighbors who had spent more than a decade living beside the wells came back with new state law on their side, and LA became the first major US city to end oil extraction for good. Arielle and Karissa also cover a record night of governor firsts, electric ferries that lift themselves out of the water, a tutoring program born in a Zimbabwe refugee camp, and a dermatologist-approved case for skipping the occasional shower. Support TWEENS on GlobalGiving: https://www.globalgiving.org/projects/transformative-education-for-refugees-in-zimbabwe/ If you have questions, comments, feedback, suggestions, or just want to say hi, send a message to: podcast@optimistdaily.com . Want to be part of the Optimism Movement? Become an Emissary . Subscribe to our FREE Daily/Weekly Newsletter and follow us on Instagram , X , and Blue Sky . The Optimist Daily is a project of the World Business Academy. Donate link: https://www.optimistdaily.com/donate-to-support-the-optimist-daily/?lsc=41ef528d Theme and all original music by Marvin Lanes Transcript: Karissa: Hello everyone, I’m Karissa Arielle: I’m Arielle Karissa: And welcome back to The Optimist Daily’s weekly roundup Arielle: Yes. What an eventful time that’s been in the States. Uh, how are you feeling, Karissa? Karissa: Yeah. An eventful week, I would say. Yeah. Um, I am feeling pretty optimistic. I know last week’s podcast episode we didn’t talk about the midterms results, but there were a lot of great election turnouts from last week that we’ll talk a little bit about in the podcast, and I feel just very hopeful. Arielle: Yeah, definitely a week full of optimism, and it’s been big news also here on the other side of the pond. So we try to keep it not so politically charged with The Optimist Daily, because there’s already so much tension when it comes to politics, and we are really trying to unite people over solutions. But that being said, a lot of our solutions do have to do with, uh, human rights and equal representation, and a lot of things that do align with, uh, the changes that could potentially be coming based on these midterms. And maybe I’ll just leave it at that. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. I mean, it takes all of us to make a difference, to make a change, and we’re more alike than we are different, and I think that kind of has prevailed in these US elections. One of my friends made a great TikTok that was just talking about how if you have American nationality, you have such a great tool to be able to vote for not only our country, but we influence so many things around the world. So it was good to see a lot of people turn out for these elections, and I’m just feeling optimistic about it. We’ll talk about that more in just a moment. But before we get to that, we want to remind you that all these solutions are available in our free daily and weekly newsletter. Arielle: You can also follow us on socials. We are @optimistdaily on everything except for X. There we are @OdeToOptimism, and we love it when you guys slide into our DMs or comment on our posts or share stories with friends and loved ones. Karissa: And of course, we want to welcome any comments, questions, or feedback on our social media channels if you want, or you can also email us at podcast@optimistdaily.com. Arielle: A huge thank you to anyone who participates and engages with us. Our Optimist community is what makes this work so meaningful and special, and we appreciate every single one of you. We especially appreciate our Emissaries who financially support The Optimist Daily and help keep this mission going forward. An Emissary is anyone who donates. It could just be a one-time donation or a regular monthly or annual donation. Every little bit helps. And this year we do have a little goal. We have already mentioned this to people who receive our newsletters. We would love to get 100 new Emissaries by the end of 2026. So we can start 2027 even stronger than we are right now. We have gotten to the halfway point, I think, Karissa. Is that correct? Karissa: Just about. So we really need this final push by the end of the year to get to our goal. This is definitely the time to give back in this giving season. And we’d really appreciate if you would help us out, if you haven’t already. And speaking of the giving season, the Local Changemaker Series is currently being published right now. And we’ll talk about this week’s Changemaker later on. We wanna, again, thank everybody who submitted a nomination for that. And it’s been such a great time giving back to The Optimist Daily community, and recognizing who makes you optimistic. Arielle: Can’t believe we only have two more features after this week, then it’s already Thanksgiving. Well, with all of that said and done, Karissa, did you want to lead us into this week’s solutions? Karissa: Yeah, I will take it from here, Arielle. 2026 midterms produced a record wave of historic governor firsts Karissa: The first solution we had this week, which we kinda were already talking about, is that “2026 midterms produced a record wave of historic governor firsts.” Last week, on November 3rd, election day, 10 states elected governors who were first. And the thing that makes this interesting is it crossed party lines completely. We’re talking a Republican first Black governor in Florida, a Democrat flipping Texas. The night didn’t tell just one story, it told 10 different ones. Just for the governors, but it told a lot of stories just across the board. One that stood out to me, and one that will definitely end up in the history books, is that Keisha Lance Bottoms in Georgia became the first Black woman ever elected governor of any US state. And in 200 years of gubernatorial elections, it had never happened. Her election was very inspirational. I believe her great-grandfather was a slave. We’ve made so much progress, so it’s still so closely… It’s not that far away, too, and we’re still— Arielle: Yeah, that past is not as far away as a lot of us like to think. Karissa: Yeah, exactly. Of course, Texas was the biggest upset of the night across the board, and that was very inspirational to see as well. Democrat Gina Hinojosa beat incumbent Greg Abbott, and it made her the first Latina governor and the first Democrat to win that race in over 30 years. It was just good to see so many different people be elected to these positions across the United States. And it just feels like we’re shaking things up a bit, and having some more accurate representation of what our country looks like. Dermatologists weigh in on the eat-your-skincare TikTok trend Karissa: Well, moving on to the next solution, we have “Dermatologists weigh in on the eat-your-skincare TikTok trend.” Before I go on, Arielle, have you heard about this trend? Arielle: I’ve seen little YouTube Shorts or my sisters will send me reels about, like, this special carrot salad that’s like you eating your retinol or something, ’cause I’m in my 30s now, so they’re just sending me all this stuff. But I, yeah, I wonder if it really does work. So this article definitely caught my attention. Karissa: If you’ve been on this eat-your-skincare side of TikTok or the internet, this is for you, but it’s also for anyone who’s been kind of skeptical about it. It turns out that dermatologists say it’s both real and over-hyped at the same time, but the nuance is actually pretty interesting. So the core thing is that food can fill the tank, but it can’t overfill it. So it means that eating more vitamin C doesn’t make your collagen-making work faster or anything. It just makes sure it’s not running low. And one aspect this article talked about is the eat your sunscreen angle of it all. It sounds kind of wild, but it actually has science behind it, which I did not know. Certain carotenoids and polyphenols have been studied for UV protection, but dermatologists are very clear that these are an extra layer and not a replacement for actual physical SPF. The foods that actually show up in dermatologists’ recommendations are ones that you would probably expect. It’s salmon, avocado, walnuts, eggs, dark chocolate. So this is kind of a vindicating solution if you’re already eating that way. It’s helping you out. It’s not gonna do a million things more for your skin, but it’ll definitely help you out. Arielle: Yeah. Okay, that’s kind of what I thought. I think food, in terms of skincare, will support the overall system, but there’s so many products. I try not to have too complicated of a skincare routine, ’cause I know that too many products is also not ideal for your skin. So if you can combine the serums, the moisturizers, the creams that work for you with a really good nutritious diet, then I think that’s gonna help you glow from the inside and the outside. Karissa: 100%. Took the words right out of my mouth. Electric ferries that fly above water are arriving in the US Karissa: The next solution is “Electric ferries that fly above water are arriving in the US.” We’ve talked about this a little bit before on The Optimist Daily. There’s these really cool electric ferries that fly. They’re kinda like skimming across the water a bit. And so the technology is that they use underwater wings to lift the hull out of the water, and that will cut the drag by 66%, makes it a lot faster, and it’s finally what makes long range electric boats practical. Over in Europe and Canada, I believe they’ve already been kinda using these for transportation. But San Francisco is about to spend half of a billion dollars converting their whole ferry fleet over to these electric ferries. The problem with electric boats has been that the drag has been bad, and so they haven’t been so quick. Water resists a vessel much more than air resists a car, so batteries couldn’t hold enough charge to make it very useful. Hydrofoils solve that by just getting the boat out of the water a bit. I’m excited to see these over in the US, and San Francisco is close to me, and though I don’t really use ferries when I’m visiting the cities, maybe I’ll have to check it out the next time I’m over. Fall activities for you and your dog: a trainer’s guide Karissa: Okay, well, this solution is another lifestyle one, and it’s “Fall activities for you and your dog: a trainer’s guide.” So this solution is a cute and fun one, but it’s essentially a permission slip to take your dog somewhere fun this fall, whether that’s the farmer’s market, pumpkin patches, corn mazes, hiking trails. We have tips from a dog trainer named Sassafras Patterdale who breaks down what to bring, what to watch for, and how to make these trips actually good for the dog and not just all about the photos. Arielle, I thought about you and Tink. Have you done anything autumn-like with her? Arielle: She’s usually off leash, and she loves sniffing around, so we do take her out on, I guess you can call them hikes or just, like, really long walks. I haven’t really taken her to farmer’s markets, which is one of the tips here. Tink is kind of… She doesn’t like kids. Karissa: So. Well, that could be a little— a little hard at the farmer’s market ’cause there usually tends to be a lot of families. And in this article, they’re kinda talking about taking your dog to the farmer’s market, aiming it at, like, younger dogs because it can be a really good training opportunity with all the people and the smells and foot traffic. So it’s kind of like a good place for younger dogs to just get more of that exposure and more practice for calm leash behavior, helping them get used to that. So maybe Tink is a little bit past that. Arielle: Yeah, she’s a bit too old for that, set in her ways. But your dog is also… Is your dog a senior dog? Karissa: Oh, yes, he is a very senior dog now, so he’s not really out on the leash in public anymore, unfortunately. But we used to take him to the farmer’s market, and I think we took him to some kind of, like, fall pumpkin patch thing at some point, and we definitely have a lot of good photos over the years of him with a cute pumpkin. So yeah, it’s just a good time of year to get your pup out there. One consistent thread and important reminder for all the activities that are mentioned in this article is to call ahead or research ahead to make sure dogs are allowed to be wherever you’re going if it’s somewhere, uh, out in public. Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap Karissa: “Brazil releases the world’s first fossil fuel phaseout roadmap.” This first global roadmap is all about phasing out coal, oil, and gas. It’s a voluntary roadmap, and it has no legal teeth, and it came out during COP30 last year, which notably ended without mentioning fossil fuels in the final text at all. The roadmap exists because Brazil decided to just do it anyways, and it’s being brought back up now that COP31 is happening as we speak. Just kind of jumping back to last year, what happened at COP30, Saudi Arabia and Russia killed the fossil fuel language, and Brazil’s response was to publish this independently and bring it into COP31 this year, which opened, uh, this week. The plan is a three-phase plan through 2033, and it explicitly says there’s no universal solution. Countries are supposed to tailor it to their own situation, which makes it harder to dismiss, but also harder to hold anyone to. Arielle: I think it is encouraging that countries are creating plans, or at least Brazil is creating a plan even though it’s not legally required of them. There’s no external motivation other than the fact that they want to help our environment survive uh, and thrive. And I think that shift from asking or requesting people to commit to the change to just giving them an example of how they can actually make the change is a good kind of reframe. Karissa: 100%. Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students Arielle: The next solution is a Local Changemakers feature. It’s titled “Prince Bashangezi turned personal loss into peer tutoring for refugee students.” This Local Changemaker story is really quite moving. Prince grew up at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe, a camp of more than 17,000 people near the Mozambique border, home to families displaced by conflict across Central and Eastern Africa. He lost his own family to war before ending up there, and he was 17 or 18-ish when COVID hit. While that was happening, he was trying to finish his A-Levels, and when schools closed, he and a small group of fellow students just started teaching the younger kids themselves, ’cause, of course, there was a lack of schooling during that time. And this eventually turned into a program called TWEENS, which stands for Together We Educationally Empower Non-privileged Students. He’s now at Pomona College in California, studying computer science and economics, and the program he built in that camp is actually still running, so it’s now been, uh, over half a decade. The Optimist who nominated Prince for the Local Changemaker series said, “Prince’s work is a reaction to his incredible loss,” and that he turned his personal tragedy into loving service for others. And that framing says everything about what TWEENS is. This peer model works in a refugee context in a way outside volunteers can’t really replicate. These tutors live in the camp. They went through the same disruptions. They understand what it means to build a future from inside a displaced population, so their credibility comes from proximity and not credentials. TWEENS has expanded to include an A-level program, a girls’ book club, and ongoing homework support alongside the original peer tutoring. If you’re interested in helping out, then the GlobalGiving campaign is still active, and I can put a link to where you can donate to this project, uh, in the show notes. This is a great story that Optimists can actually do something about right now, so if you feel compelled to learn more or to give, then I would highly recommend just checking out the article. The dermatologist guide to a skin-friendly shower routine Arielle: The next solution is another skin solution. It’s titled “The dermatologist guide to a skin-friendly shower routine.” Three dermatologists are out here saying that showering every day might be working against your skin. They’re not saying it in, like, a soft, “Well, maybe,” kind of way. They’re actually pretty direct about it. This piece breaks down who actually needs daily showers, who doesn’t, and what the signs are that you’ve overdone it, because that squeaky clean feeling after a hot shower, you might think, “Oh, yeah, I got everything. I’m, like, completely clean.” But that’s not necessarily a good sign. Karissa, are you a shower every day type of person? Karissa: I mean, I definitely am, and I do a lot of heated workouts where I’m sweating a lot, so I definitely need my daily shower, but I’m so intrigued of the argument against it. What about you, Arielle? Arielle: I used to be a shower every day when I was living under my mom’s, uh, watchful eye, and definitely whenever I live in a tropical place, that’s, like, multiple showers a day ’cause I’m sweating, and it’s, like, kind of grimy, and you get sand and everything everywhere. But now I have to say I don’t shower every single day. If I don’t work out that day, and I don’t really do anything strenuous, then chances are, I’m probably gonna skip the shower. Karissa: Yeah. Arielle: Okay, so this article makes a key distinction. Hygiene and skin health are not the same thing. So daily washing serves hygiene, but when you think about it, if you’re not super active, then only your underarms, your groin, your feet, and the skin folds that, like, trap a lot of, I guess, like, perspiration and stuff, that’s what needs soap every day. The rest of your body, you can usually skip. The signs that your skin is asking for a break are quite specific. So if your skin feels super tight after the shower or if you’re experiencing persistent nighttime itchiness or ashiness or flaking on your shins, that’s what a stripped skin barrier looks like. All the listeners out there, you guys should just check those things out and see if any of that applies to you. There’s something about age here as well, ’cause age actually changes the whole game when it comes to showering. Babies, like, they can’t be showered all the time. Their skin is too sensitive, so twice a week is good for babies, whereas teens, on the other hand, they’re going through a lot of hormonal fluctuations. They’re going through puberty. They need more showers, for sure. And then older adults often need less showers because the skin produces fewer surface oils over time, and you just have to kind of use your own judgment. Uh, this is not a one-size-fits-all solution. There are some key tips that I’m glazing over right now, but you can find everything in the article. After a decade of community pressure, LA bans oil drilling for good Arielle: The next solution is titled “After a decade of community pressure, LA bans oil drilling for good.” Los Angeles just became the first major US city to ban oil extraction entirely, and what makes this story different from most environmental news is the decade of community advocacy that actually got it done. This wasn’t a top-down policy decision. People who are actually living next to oil wells pushed for this for more than 10 years. The neighborhoods where these wells sit are working-class communities of color. Residents have been living with benzene and hydrogen sulfide and higher rates of respiratory illness for generations. Wendy Miranda, one of the lead advocates, has asthma, and so does her mother. The city actually tried this back in 2022, but they just passed an ordinance. Oil companies challenged it in court, and they won. So California then passed legislation giving local governments more power, and this vote is what came out the other side. Environmental justice has shifted from an advocacy framework to a legal one, and these days, communities have better tools than they did 10 years ago. And then I also noticed that in the article, the communities expressed that they’re not necessarily anti-oil. They’re anti-drilling next to our kids’ school. And this framing could resonate more broadly than just the pure climate messaging, so they’re also positioning themselves in a much more strategic way. This isn’t just an environmental issue. It’s a health issue, and it’s a human rights issue. Karissa: I’m glad to see this pass in LA because, yeah, I don’t think anyone should have to live right next to a oil drilling well. The next challenge is going to be removing these oil wells because I don’t think there’s, like, a great legal framework for holding oil companies accountable for either paying for that cleanup or removing them. They’ve had a couple of oil wells in the area that have just, like, sat there for years, and getting those out of the way is also the next step here. Why spiders show up in your home every fall, and what to do about it Arielle: The next solution is very seasonal. It’s titled “Why spiders show up in your home every fall, and what to do about it.” Karissa: Oh, I need this solution. I think I have, like, two spider bites on my ankles, so. Arielle: Oh, you have actual bites? I just have so many spiders, like up in the corners of my… Well, basically all the rooms in my house. So yeah, this article gets into it, and if you are like me and Karissa and you’ve been seeing more spiders lately, there’s a simple biological reason. Fall is mating season for spiders, and a lot of them are coming inside to find mates and somewhere quiet to lay their eggs. And the reassuring thing an entomologist from Oregon State said is that most of them are minding their own business. They’re also eating your gnats and all those other insects that might be bothering you in your home. I found it unexpected that of the 3,700 spider species in the United States, only 0.3% are dangerous to humans. The ones showing up in your house are almost certainly not in that category, thankfully. The entry points are pretty mundane. You could probably guess. Your worn garage door weather strip, cracks in your foundation, gaps around window frames are all entry points for spiders and other critters. And if your house already has like a lot of gnats or flies, then the spiders are just following the food. Karissa: Yeah. That makes sense. Arielle: The most effective seasonal fix is clearing wood piles or compost heaps and old boards from around the perimeter of your house because that’s where spiders can shelter before they come into your home. There’s fall decluttering content everywhere right now, and this article gives it a practical reason beyond just aesthetics. But there’s also a maybe just leave them kind of framing at the end of this article, and it’s part of a broader shift towards coexisting with nature rather than trying to eliminate it. Because the spiders are cold, they just wanna get cozy, they wanna find a mate. It’s cuffing season for them as well, I guess. I used to be super scared of spiders, but I think they’ve… I don’t know. We don’t have like really juicy-looking spiders here in the Netherlands. They’re all kind of like spindly, and they look really fragile. Ah. I don’t know, maybe in Northern California it’s a bit of a different story. Karissa: Yeah. They’re pretty small. Like, obviously you won’t ever want one around. I did see a pretty juicy one though the other day on the wall, and it was a little bit scary. But usually the ones that end up in my house here are not too bad. But yeah, I think there’s some kind of one that like bites, ’cause every once in a while I’ll just have like this giant, like welt from… That’s what I’ve heard, read. I never see the spider doing it, but yeah, my ankle currently has a bite, so it’s a little bit annoying, but it’s nothing like poisonous of course. I guess I’ll take this advice and this solution to let them coexist. How two Princeton graduates built the world’s first microplastics removal system Arielle: All right. The last solution that I’m going to be sharing with all you Optimists this week is titled “How two Princeton graduates built the world’s first microplastics removal system.” There is now a wastewater treatment plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, that removes microplastics before they reach the ocean, and it’s the first one in the entire world. The two people who built the technology are architects who basically looked at how certain wetland plants trap microplastics naturally, and then scaled it up. There’s, again, no law that’s requiring this, but they just did it anyway. The design philosophy is explicitly about simplicity. The founders wanted something like an iPhone approach to a complex problem. Minimal material, low energy, but big results. It’s a pretty big problem, these microplastics. They’ve already turned up in human bloodstream, in brain tissue and other organs. And the Atlantic County plant manager said it pretty plainly, “We’re discharging to the ocean. If we’re not removing the plastic, we’re putting it back in.” And yeah, it’s just like the, the Brazil, uh, phase out fossil fuels roadmap. There’s no law that’s requiring this. It’s the municipality doing it because it’s the right thing to do, not because they have to. Karissa: Yeah. This is so awesome, and it’s very intriguing that it’s the first in the world to do this. I know we’ve written on The Optimist Daily about a lot of solutions that can filter out microplastics and being developed, but I guess we haven’t really seen them deployed so much. So this is a great, uh, article describing how this is actually being put into action now. And the fact that they don’t have to, they’re doing it to better their municipality is, uh, is great news. Arielle: All right. Well, those were all the solutions that we had to share with everyone this week. But as usual, we leave you off with a positive quote. Karissa: This week we have, “If they don’t give you a seat at the table, bring a folding chair.” And that’s from Shirley Chisholm. I really like this one, and I was inspired to add it just from all the great progress in the United States we saw in this past week of people getting a seat at the table. So I’m excited to see what those seats will produce. Arielle: Well, Karissa and I wish everyone a wonderful, restful weekend. Uh, we will be back next week with more solutions. But in the meantime, stay positive and optimistic. Karissa: Absolutely. Have a great weekend, everyone. Bye! The post Podcast Transcript November 13th, 2026— This midterm’s historic governor firsts, flying electric ferries, and eat-your-skincare first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News .

items.descriptionOriginal: On a Saturday morning at a government school in Bengaluru's Mullur Colony, 17-year-old Asavari Agrawal barely gets through the gate before the children surround her. Some run up to hug her. Others tug at her hands, eager to show her something or pull her into a game. The younger ones often cling to her, refusing to let go even as she tries to begin the day's activities. By now, the scene is familiar. Asavari greets the teachers and children, gets everyone moving and settles into whatever the morning calls for. There may be table tennis, an art activity, a lesson, a fitness session or simply time spent talking and playing. "When she enters the gate, they run to her," says Victoria, headmistress of the school. "In the beginning they were shy. But because she came every week, they became comfortable very quickly." At 17, Asavari is balancing Class 12 , college applications, national-level table tennis, Bharatanatyam and Grade 8 piano. Yet for nearly five years, she has also made space for spending her weekends with children at government schools and residential homes across Bengaluru. For the children at Mullur Colony Government School, Saturday mornings mean games, activities and time with their favourite Didi. That commitment began when she was a child herself and eventually grew into Shape the Future, the youth-led initiative she founded at 13. Today, around 50 student volunteers are part of the wider network, reaching roughly 250 children. There have been sports sessions, health and eye camps, menstrual hygiene drives, book collections and learning activities. But when Asavari talks about what matters most, she does not begin with those numbers. "I think the idea of showing up is what matters most to my NGO," she says. "No matter how many drives or fundraisers or events that I hold, I feel like being there for the kids, emotionally and physically, matters the most." It started with playdates Asavari's connection with children from underserved communities began long before Shape the Future. When she was young, her mother began volunteering at Karuna Shreya hospice after experiencing several personal losses. Asavari would accompany her and, over time, also began visiting Thayi Mane, a government-recognised home for orphaned and destitute children. Back then, she did not think of herself as a volunteer. "I was really small when I started going there," she recalls. "Honestly, initially it was like playdates for me. It was so fun going there and playing with the kids." From table tennis and fitness sessions to art and learning activities, Asavari and her volunteers create opportunities for children to explore new interests. As she grew older, those visits began to look different. She started noticing the opportunities she had access to, from learning sports and dancing to playing the piano, and how different that access could be for the children she was meeting. In 2021, that realisation took a more concrete form. Asavari had started her own table tennis academy and decided to take the sport to the children she had been visiting. She brought tables, rackets, balls, shoes, clothes, jackets and fitness equipment and conducted a session for around 100 children. For many, table tennis was unfamiliar. "I think they were really excited to learn a new sport that they probably hadn't heard of yet," she says. The first session was not easy. Asavari was around the same age as many of the children and had to introduce a completely new sport to a large group. But some children took to it quickly, and the experience made her think about what else she could bring to them. Asavari believes that showing up consistently and building relationships with children matters more than organising one-off donation drives. A year later, in 2022, she started Shape the Future. What began with one sport slowly expanded into a broader effort to give children access to learning, play and experiences that might otherwise remain outside their everyday lives. What a Saturday looks like Today, a typical weekend begins with Asavari and her volunteers packing supplies for the day's session. Depending on the activity, that could mean sports equipment, stationery, educational material or art supplies. Around 10 to 15 volunteers may join her, although the group changes because they are all school students managing their own academic schedules. There is usually a warm-up, the main activity and plenty of time for games before everyone heads home. The session may last only a couple of hours, but it has become a regular part of Asavari's week. "I have a lot of exams and applications and personal work," she says. "But setting aside one or two hours every weekend doesn't do any harm. It's not like work to me. It's more of a hobby going there." With around 50 student volunteers, Shape the Future now reaches nearly 250 children across Bengaluru. At Mullur Colony, Victoria has seen that commitment first-hand. "Most Saturdays she comes herself. On some Saturdays when she cannot come, her team comes, but someone is always here every Saturday without fail," she says. That consistency has changed the relationship between Asavari and the children. "When she first came, they would just silently follow what she said," Victoria recalls. "Now they talk back, they argue, they pull her, they sit close to her. This closeness takes time. It comes only because she has been here every week." Aparna, in-charge and principal at Thayi Mane and Lakshya Residential School, has witnessed the same bond. "They know each one by name," she says. "They wait for her on Saturday. When she comes, they run to her." Why a missed Saturday matters to the children There are two kindergarten girls at Mullur Colony, Aarohi and Anjali, whom Asavari has grown particularly close to. When she arrives, they often run towards her and refuse to let go. "They keep calling me Didi, they keep calling me Amma," Asavari says. "We've built such a close connection with these kids that it just hurts me to not end up going there." For Asavari, the most meaningful part of volunteering is the trust she has built with children who now look forward to seeing her every Saturday. Then there is Sumit, a boy who recently lost both his parents. One day, he told Asavari, "You're the only family I have left now." For a teenager who is still learning how to understand grief, moments like this can be difficult to process. "I think I'm still too young to understand each and every kid's emotion," she says. "But I try." At Thayi Mane, Aparna remembers another moment. When Asavari had surgery on her appendix, she could not visit for several weeks. When she finally returned, a boy named Partha told her that one night his "heart pained" because he thought she might not come back. "She did not say anything. She just held him," Aparna recalls. These experiences have shaped Asavari's understanding of volunteering . She has seen people arrive for one-off activities, donate something, take photographs and leave. For children who have experienced people coming and going, that can make it difficult to trust that someone will stay. Sumit, who recently lost both his parents, found a sense of belonging in Asavari. "The best and worst part is getting attached to these kids," she says. The children have even told her that when she does not come, they worry she might leave like others have. "They don't look for money. They don't look for items," Asavari says. "They look for someone who isn't going to give up on them." For her, that means treating the children as equals rather than beneficiaries. "It's about not treating them like a project. Treating them as equals and constantly building that relationship." When the children asked for books The library at Mullur Colony grew out of these everyday conversations. Asavari would ask the children what they wanted to learn about, what they dreamed of becoming and what they wished they could read. Their answers revealed a simple gap: they wanted to explore beyond their school textbooks, but there were very few books available to them. So Asavari and her team began collecting them. Over nearly two years, five student volunteers took charge of the collection, reaching out to schools and communities and bringing in donated books. Slowly, the collection grew to more than 2,000. Asavari and her team transformed an unused room at the government school into a library, complete with bookshelves, furniture and reading material. The school also had a room that had essentially become a storage space. Turning it into a library meant redoing the flooring, repainting the walls, cleaning the room, adding shelves and furniture, and finally sorting and arranging the books. "It went from being an absolute rag of a room," Asavari says. "We had to uproot the entire flooring, repaint the walls, clean the entire room and then bring in the furniture and the books." For Victoria, who has watched the school change since Shape the Future first arrived in 2024, the library represents something the children simply did not have before. "Before this we had nothing. Only textbooks. No library, nothing like that," she says. "She collected more than two thousand books and arranged the room also with shelves and light. For our school this is a very big thing ." The idea has also been about understanding what individual children want to read rather than simply filling a room with books. At Thayi Mane, one girl wanted more advanced reading material, so Asavari sourced a set of 25 encyclopaedias specifically for her. "That kind of attention is rare," Aparna says. "The children feel seen when someone notices what they individually need." Preparing for the Saturdays she may miss Shape the Future has remained entirely bootstrapped. Asavari has funded its work through earnings from her Bharatanatyam Arangetram, table tennis prize money and even by selling her own piano and table tennis table. But she does not see those decisions as sacrifices. "I wouldn't call myself selfless," she says. "I think the kids needed it more than I did." If anything, the harder thing to give has been time. And now, time is precisely what Asavari is preparing to have less of. She is in Class 12 and hopes to study at university in the US or UK. For the first time since she began visiting these children regularly, she may soon be unable to walk through the school gates every Saturday. "I'm absolutely terrified as to how these kids are going to feel once I leave," she says. "When I'm in college, I'm not going to be able to come for months." So she is preparing Shape the Future to continue without her. Responsibilities have been divided among heads of fundraising, volunteering, social media and operations, while younger students are being given more responsibility. Asavari is deliberately preparing a team that can continue the work even when she is away. Her mother, who first introduced her to volunteering, remains part of that support system too. "This is not just Asavari's work," Aparna says. "Her mother has always been part of this. This is their family's commitment." Asavari describes what she hopes to build in a different way. "I think of it like generational wealth," she says. "You build it, you pass it on, you make sure it outlasts you." As she prepares to leave for university, Asavari is training younger volunteers to ensure Shape the Future continues even in her absence. What began as playdates now includes dozens of young volunteers, hundreds of children and a library built from thousands of donated books. Yet what Asavari values most cannot be measured in numbers. It is the familiarity of a Saturday morning, the children knowing she will walk through the gate, and the trust that has grown because she has kept returning. "I've just done it consistently," she says. "And I've grown it into something big. These little changes, being consistent with these little changes, is what matters most." Her advice to other young people is just as simple. "You don't need to build the world's biggest NGO. Start with 10 children, but stay." All images courtesy of Asavari Agrawal

items.descriptionOriginal: The advice for eating in a warming world is by now familiar: more beans, fruit and vegetables; less meat and dairy. But it seems the same plate could also help with an entirely different planetary problem. Two new studies in mice suggest that high-fiber diets help nanoplastics, the tiny plastic particles strewn through oceans and soils, and found in the food we eat, pass through the gut without being absorbed. High-fat diets, by contrast, appear to make the body hold onto more of them. Millions of tons of plastic waste enter the environment each year. This waste slowly degrades into microplastics and nanoplastics that find their way into farms, plants, ocean life, and even the Amazon—where they were recently found in the blood of wild tapirs and anteaters . Once ingested with food, these tiny particles percolate into the human brain, lungs, liver, kidneys, placenta, and testes , where they cause inflammation, oxidative stress, DNA damage, and other cellular injuries. Nanoplastics are even found in the atherosclerotic plaques of our coronary arteries , where they increase the risk of heart attack, stroke, or premature death by more than 4-fold. The two new studies looked at how diet influences the absorption and effects of nanoplastics in mice. One study found that in the first 24 hours after consuming nanoplastics, mice eating medium- or high-fiber diets accumulated two to seven times less plastics in their intestinal tract than those on regular diets. Mice fed nanoplastics for 28 days experienced inflammation and breakdown of their intestinal barriers—setting the stage for nanoplastics to enter the rest of the body; but these negative effects were absorption of nanoplastics by 2.8-fold compared to regular diets. That finding is especially worrisome, given that fast foods and takeout foods, both rich in fat, are often served in containers laced with plastics. In the two new studies, dietary fiber may have exerted its protective effects by shaping the intestinal microbiome, coating the nanoplastic particles, and speeding up their elimination through poop—allowing the intestinal lining to avoid excessive exposure. These new insights come at a time when scientists are already proposing higher-plant and lower-animal diets that could improve worldwide health while also reducing the environmental impacts of the global food system , such as greenhouse emissions, water pollution, and land use. Human studies are needed to confirm these newest results. But for the moment, they suggest that sustainable diets could also reduce another nasty problem: nanoplastics. items.descriptionOriginal: What if your biggest worry in old age is not who will look after you, but who will look after the person you love when you’re gone? This is the moving story behind Pyre, filmmaker Vinod Kapri’s award-winning film set in an almost-deserted Himalayan village. In 2018, Vinod met an elderly couple in Munsiyari, Uttarakhand, whose livelihood depended on their goats. The husband said their income helped him arrange for people to carry his ailing wife downhill for medical care. As long as he had his goats, he said, his wife would survive. But his biggest fear was who would care for her if he died first. His wife’s worry was just as moving: who would cook for him, since he didn’t know how? These simple yet profound answers stayed with Vinod for years, inspiring him to tell a story about love, ageing, loneliness and an elderly couple’s arduous wait for their estranged son. Starring first-time actors Padam Singh Kapri, a retired Army serviceman, and Heera Devi, Pyre was made with limited resources. With no big studio backing, Vinod exhausted his savings and even sold his car and a plot of land to finance the film. After winning 18 international awards, including multiple Best Film honours, Pyre finally made its way to Indian theatres on 30 October. Have you caught it on the big screen yet? #VinodKapri #PyreFilm #IndianCinema #IndependentCinema #Uttarakhand

items.descriptionOriginal: Your height is one number. Your weight is another. Put them together and you get your BMI. But is that enough to understand your weight and health? Not by itself. BMI is a useful screening measure. But it doesn’t directly tell us how much of your weight is muscle or fat, or where that fat is stored. That is where your waist adds context, giving us a view of abdominal fat distribution that can be relevant to cardiometabolic risk. So should you trust your waist more than your BMI? Not really. They give different information, and neither is a diagnosis on its own. If they seem to tell different stories, don’t try to diagnose yourself. Bring both to a qualified doctor. Use them as a reason to have a conversation, not to judge yourself. Keep up balanced meals, regular movement, strength activity and good sleep. BMI and waist are starting points, not verdicts. Talk to a qualified doctor about your weight-management needs. This is general information, not a diagnosis or medical advice. #CountWhatMatters #BMI #WaistMeasurement #KnowYourNumbers #MetabolicHealth [BMI vs waist measurement, what does BMI tell you, is BMI enough, waist size and health risk, body composition India]

items.descriptionOriginal: Every winter, Delhi struggles with worsening air pollution . As smog settles over the city, efforts to clear the air raise an unusual possibility. What if it rained? Could artificial rain wash away pollutants and make the air easier to breathe? The idea gained attention after the United Arab Emirates (UAE) invested in cloud seeding, a technique that encourages existing clouds to produce rainfall. Research in the region has also highlighted how rain can reduce airborne dust and particulate matter. This raised hopes that the same technology could help Delhi tackle its pollution. In October 2025, the Delhi government partnered with the Indian Institute of Technology (IIT) Kanpur to conduct a cloud-seeding experiment. However, the operation failed to produce meaningful rainfall in the capital. So, why did a technique associated with improved air quality in Dubai fail in Delhi? The answer lies in differences in weather conditions, cloud formation, and the limitations of cloud seeding. What happened in Dubai? The UAE has invested in cloud seeding for decades to increase rainfall in a country that receives very little natural precipitation. Its programme primarily aims to improve water security and replenish groundwater. Every winter, Delhi struggles with worsening air pollution. Photograph: (Image generated by AI) Researchers have also examined whether rainfall could help reduce air pollution in the region. A study published in the journal Environmental Pollution examined atmospheric dust and particulate matter around Dubai and Abu Dhabi. It found that dust storms contributed to higher concentrations of suspended particles, while rainfall helped bring these levels down. A January 2021 report by The National highlighted these findings. When raindrops fall through the atmosphere, they collect suspended particles and carry them towards the ground. This process, known as wet deposition, helps remove some pollutants from the air. However, the research established the benefits of rainfall in reducing airborne dust. It did not conclusively prove that cloud seeding alone was responsible for improving Dubai's air quality. How does cloud seeding work? Cloud seeding does not create clouds or produce rain from a clear sky. It works by introducing tiny particles into existing clouds to encourage water droplets or ice crystals to grow. Depending on the cloud type and atmospheric conditions, scientists use materials such as silver iodide or salts, including sodium chloride and potassium chloride. These particles act as nuclei around which water droplets or ice crystals form . As the droplets grow heavier, they may eventually fall as rain. The UAE uses specially equipped aircraft to release seeding materials into suitable clouds. However, the technique needs naturally occurring clouds with sufficient moisture. According to the World Meteorological Organization , cloud seeding cannot create rain clouds or bring moisture into an otherwise dry atmosphere. Cloud seeding does not create clouds or produce rain from a clear sky. Photograph: (Reuters) Why did the experiment fail in Delhi? On 28 October 2025, aircraft carrying cloud-seeding flares conducted two sorties over parts of Delhi, including Burari, Karol Bagh, and Mayur Vihar. The experiment was part of a pilot project undertaken by the Delhi government in collaboration with IIT Kanpur. However, it did not produce rainfall in Delhi. Only negligible precipitation was recorded in neighbouring Noida and Greater Noida, at 0.1 mm and 0.2 mm respectively. The biggest obstacle was insufficient moisture in the clouds. According to NDTV's report on the experiment , IIT Kanpur director Manindra Agarwal explained that the clouds had moisture levels of around 15 to 20 percent, which were insufficient to trigger the desired rainfall. A second attempt scheduled for 29 October was also put on hold because atmospheric conditions were unsuitable. The problem was not simply the technology or the material released by the aircraft. The clouds themselves lacked the conditions needed to produce rain. Delhi's winter weather adds to the challenge Delhi's weather makes cloud seeding particularly difficult during the months when pollution is at its worst. During winter, the city frequently experiences low wind speeds, temperature inversions, and limited atmospheric mixing. These conditions trap pollutants close to the ground instead of allowing them to disperse. At the same time, the atmosphere often lacks the moisture and suitable cloud formations required for artificial rainfall. A study by IIT Delhi researchers titled 'Can Cloud Seeding Help Tackle Delhi's Air Pollution?' examined weather and pollution data collected between 2011 and 2021. The researchers found that suitable conditions for cloud seeding are relatively uncommon during Delhi's winter pollution season. Western disturbances, which bring moisture and precipitation to north-western India, can occasionally create favourable conditions. However, these opportunities are limited. The researchers concluded that cloud seeding could be considered an emergency measure when suitable weather conditions exist, but it cannot serve as a dependable pollution-control strategy. Can artificial rain really clear the air? Rainfall can help remove suspended particles, but the relief is generally temporary. Depending on the cloud type and atmospheric conditions, scientists use materials such as silver iodide or salts, including sodium chloride and potassium chloride. Photograph: (Newsonair) The IIT Delhi research found that heavy rainfall can wash out PM2.5 and PM10 more effectively than light rainfall. However, pollutant concentrations can return to earlier levels within one to five days as vehicles, industries, and other sources continue releasing emissions. Delhi's pollution comes from several sources, including vehicular exhaust, construction dust, industrial emissions, waste burning, and agricultural residue burning. Even if cloud seeding successfully produces rain, it cannot stop these sources from adding fresh pollutants to the atmosphere. There is also no conclusive evidence that cloud seeding consistently improves air quality in every region. A 2022 study published in the International Journal of Environmental Science and Technology examined particulate matter during cloud-seeding operations in the UAE and raised questions about the possible contribution of seeding materials to airborne particles. What does this mean for Delhi? Dubai's experience shows how rainfall can help remove airborne dust, but it does not establish cloud seeding as a reliable way to reduce AQI. Delhi's failed experiment highlights an important limitation. Technology can encourage clouds to produce rain, but it cannot compensate for unsuitable weather conditions. On 28 October 2025, aircraft carrying cloud-seeding flares conducted two sorties over parts of Delhi, including Burari, Karol Bagh, and Mayur Vihar. Photograph: (India Weekly) Cloud seeding may offer temporary relief when sufficient moisture and suitable clouds are available. For Delhi, cleaner air will depend less on waiting for artificial rain and more on preventing pollutants from entering the atmosphere in the first place. Better control of vehicle emissions, construction dust, industrial pollution, and agricultural burning will do far more for long-term air quality than waiting for the right clouds to arrive.

items.descriptionOriginal: Grief has a way of ambushing us in ordinary places. It was in the middle of an Ikea store, surrounded by display of sofas and couples building lives together, that a recently widowed woman sat down and wept. A passing stranger stopped, pressed a packet of tissues into her hands, rested a palm on her shoulder, and waited in silence until a nod signaled she was steadier. Then, she simply walked on. That wordless exchange, offered without expectation or introduction, cracked something open: "I knew then that a relationship was possible, because there are good people in the world." What followed, over the next decade, was a new love, a rebuilt life, and a quiet personal ritual -- the widow now carries tissues wherever she goes and has pressed them into the hands of four strangers crying in restaurants and bars. Kindness, it turns out, doesn't just comfort; it teaches, and those who receive it often become its most faithful carriers.

items.descriptionOriginal: Daniel Te, an American artist living in London, has set his sights on sketching distinctive landmarks at the city’s 272 active Tube stations. The 27-year-old recently completed all 16 stops on the Victoria Line in a 10-hour sketching marathon, beginning with Brixton and concluding with Walthamstow Central. He spent about half an hour at each stop drawing something near the station. Daniel Te / SWNS “I think drawing landmarks helps create a more distinctive sense of what a place is exactly,” he told SWNS. “Seven Sisters was the most memorable, and I really like the origin story — it’s the symbol of the place, just seven trees in a circle.” Te said he was surprised by what he discovered, not having researched the stations in advance. For example, at Highbury & Islington, he spotted a green plaque marking where George Orwell used to live. “And that’s something that I never knew,” he remarked. Daniel Te / SWNS When he got to the final stop at Walthamstow Central, it was getting dark and hard to see what he was sketching. “I felt relieved, hungry, tired, and satisfied,” Te said. “It was fulfilling, and I really liked the journey.” And despite increasing costs of transport, his day of traveling cost him less than $10. Daniel Te / SWNS Te moved to London from Portland, Oregon, in July, inspired to explore European city planning. “One of the reasons why I started doing Tube sketching is that I wanted to see more of London and have an excuse to go out and about,” he explained, adding, “I really do love the process of just exploring every single destination.” He has visited many cities, including Amsterdam, Vienna, and Prague, and has completed drawings of Berlin’s S7 S-Bahn and the Palace of Culture and Science in Warsaw. Whenever he sketches, he likes that people come and talk to him, share their own art, or simply watch him in action. Daniel Te / SWNS Next up? Te is inviting fellow Londoners to join him at Farringdon Station at 11 a.m. tomorrow to begin sketching the Circle Line. And further down the line (pun intended), he plans to turn the sketches into a book or expand his work to cover other locations. This article was originally written by Tahira Amini for SWNS — the U.K.’s largest independent news agency, providing globally relevant original, verified, and engaging content to the world’s leading media outlets.

items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM For decades, wastewater treatment plants have been filtering out bacteria, chemicals, and biological waste before discharging treated water back into the environment. Microplastics have been going straight through. This week, a plant in Atlantic City, New Jersey, became the first in the world to do something about that, installing a system built specifically to capture microplastics before they reach the ocean. As of this moment, no law requires this. PolyGone Systems , a startup founded by two former Princeton University graduate students, built it anyway. Why microplastics are hard to remove Plastics don’t biodegrade; they break down into tinier and tinier fragments called microplastics, which don’t go away and build up in living organisms over time. Standard wastewater treatment removes a lot, but it wasn’t designed for particles this small or this plentiful. They get into the water from industrial discharge, stormwater picking up particles shed from car tires, and washing machines releasing microfibers from synthetic clothes. By the time water arrives at a treatment plant, the microplastics are already in it. “We’re discharging to the ocean,” said Matt DeNafo, president of the Atlantic County Utilities Authority. “So, if we’re not removing the plastic that’s in our wastewater, we’re putting it back into the environment. It’s getting into the fish that we’re eating, even the water that we’re bathing. So, it really becomes an issue for human health.” Microplastics and nanoplastics have already turned up in human bloodstream, brain tissue , and other organs. Some researchers have linked exposure to a higher risk of heart attack or stroke, though scientists are still working out exactly what harm these particles cause at different levels of exposure. How the technology works PolyGone’s founders, Nathaniel Banks and Yidian Liu , trained as architects, and the technology they built shows it. Their system, called Polypods, doesn’t try to filter microplastics out of water the conventional way. Instead, it replicates the surface of ultrahydrophobic plants found in wetlands, which microplastics cling to naturally. Scale that up, and you can pull microplastics out of a water stream with very little material and minimal energy. The lab numbers are strong: more than 98 percent of microplastics removed. There’s no commercial data yet, but Banks and Liu say the Polypods work best on the smallest particles, which are also the hardest to catch by other means and the ones most easily absorbed by living tissue. Liu on the design philosophy: “We really like how some sleek products such as the iPhone were able to resolve very complex problems with very simple but sleek-looking designs. And we want to really emphasize that in how we design the Polypods.” “I think this really marks a new era for treatment innovation, where we’re able to build very large, scalable systems that use a very small amount of material and very low energy to treat very challenging contaminants,” Banks said. “And, having the first system in the world for that in Atlantic County, it’s quite unusual.” Where PolyGone goes from here A similar installation is already running at a wastewater plant in California, and PolyGone is developing a residential version. The Atlantic City system was fully funded by a federal grant, and both the technology and the funding route could give other municipalities a path to act without waiting on a mandate. items.description: ΑΠΟ ΤΗΝ ΚΑΘΗΜΕΡΙΝΗ ΣΥΝΤΑΚΤΙΚΗ ΟΜΑΔΑ OPTIMIST Εάν έχετε παρατηρήσει περισσότερες αράχνες τον τελευταίο καιρό, κοντά σε κουφώματα, πίσω από κουτιά στο γκαράζ, να κρύβονται στις γωνίες του υπογείου, δεν το φαντάζεστε. Το φθινόπωρο είναι περίοδος ζευγαρώματος για τις αράχνες, κάτι που τις κάνει πιο δραστήριες από το συνηθισμένο, και όταν πέφτουν οι θερμοκρασίες, πολλές από αυτές κάνουν το ίδιο που θα κάνατε και κατευθύνονται προς τα μέσα. Του ρ…
items.descriptionOriginal: BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM If you’ve noticed more spiders lately, near window frames, behind boxes in the garage, lurking in basement corners, you’re not imagining it. Fall is mating season for spiders , which makes them more active than usual, and when temperatures drop, many of them make the same call you would and head inside. Of the roughly 3,700 spider species in the United States, only about 0.3 percent are dangerous to humans. The rest are, in the words of Oregon State University Extension horticulturist Brooke Edmunds , “minding their own business.” Two things converging in the spiderverse It’s not only the cold driving these arachnids indoors. Spiders like cellar spiders, wolf spiders, and hobo spiders move indoors as temperatures fall, and once inside, many are also looking for mates and somewhere quiet to leave their eggs . “Just like us, they’re coming inside to get warm,” Edmunds explains. “They aren’t aggressive toward people, not even the spiders.” Some females carry egg sacs on their bodies; others are hunting for corners, furniture undersides, the back of a closet, anywhere spider silk can hold a sac in place. That’s part of why fall can feel like a sudden invasion when it’s really just two instincts running in parallel. What makes your home The Destination Some of it is biology, and some of it is a gap in the garage door seal. If the weather strip at the bottom is worn or the door doesn’t sit flush, that’s an open invitation. Same goes for cracks along the foundation and gaps around window frames. And if your house already has gnats, flies, aphids, or termites, spiders will follow, because those critters happen to make up a great menu for our eight-legged friends. Outside, what’s close to the house does a lot of the inviting. Colorado State University’s entomology experts recommend clearing away rock piles, wood stacks, old boards, and compost heaps from around the perimeter. Spiders go for dark, damp, undisturbed spots. Tree limbs that touch or hang near windows are another way in, and crawl spaces packed with boxes are definitely attractive to them. How to keep them out Caulking cracks in your foundation and making sure screens and door seals are intact does a lot. Fall is also a good time to go through basements, garages, and closets, not for tidiness, but because those neglected corners are exactly what spiders are looking for. If you’re digging into old cardboard boxes or boots that haven’t moved since last winter, wear gloves. Spiders have sometimes made a cozy home inside them. If you’d rather not evict the ones already there, that’s fine too. They’re eating the insects you’d otherwise be swatting at, and most will move on once the season turns anyway. items.descriptionOriginal: In the search for a sustainable alternative to today’s lithium-ion batteries, researchers often look to materials found readily in nature . And in the latest such advance, researchers in Spain have made a rechargeable battery that uses vitamin B12 as a catalyst. Vitamin B12 is an essential nutrient that the body needs for making red blood cells and maintaining the nervous system. The human body doesn’t naturally produce vitamin B12, and it is usually obtained from animal products such as fish, meat, and dairy. The food and drug industry cultivate bacteria that produce vitamin B12 for supplements and additives. The team from the University of Cordoba decided to put the vitamin to use in zinc-air batteries. Metal-air batteries are more sustainable than lithium-ion batteries, which rely on expensive critical minerals that are mined with an environmental and ethical cost. Metal–air batteries consist of a negative electrode made of pure metal such as lithium, magnesium, aluminum, or zinc. The positive electrode has a porous structure that lets in oxygen from the air, and a catalyst at the electrode triggers electrochemical reactions with the oxygen. “Precisely because it uses atmospheric oxygen, one of the battery’s active materials is not located inside the battery itself, thus significantly reducing its weight,” the researchers write in a paper published in the Journal of Materials Chemistry A . So metal–air batteries can pack much more energy by weight than conventional lithium-ion batteries. This makes them promising for applications where light weight is crucial, such as drones or medical devices. Indeed, small zinc-air batteries, the most practical among the different types of metal–air batteries, are used widely for hearing aids. But those medical device batteries are not rechargeable. .IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby .postImageUrl , .IRPP_ruby .centered-text-area {height: auto;position: relative;}.IRPP_ruby , .IRPP_ruby:hover , turn your house into a battery The Cordoba team wanted to make a rechargeable battery using a biomolecule. They have previously made batteries with the protein hemoglobin and the enzyme catalase, which contain iron. This time they chose vitamin B12, also called cobalamin. The vitamin contains cobalt (III) at its core, which would be essential for electrochemical reactions. Vitamin B12 is a highly soluble vitamin. To make it stable inside a battery that operates with water-based electrolytes, the team fixed it to the surface of carbon nanotubes, which are microscopic tubes made of carbon atoms. Then the researchers incorporated the nanotubes into the air electrode of alkaline zinc-air batteries. The electrodes reached a specific capacity of 199.4 mAh of energy per gram, giving rechargeable batteries with high performance. And the electrodes worked in a cyclic fashion, allowing for a battery that could be recharged for up to 250 cycles. The performance is far from what is needed for practical applications right now, but the work highlights biomolecular platforms as “a high-performance and sustainable frontier for next-generation rechargeable batteries,” writes the team. items.title: Φανταζόμαστε τις ποώδεις πόλεις του μέλλοντος
items.titleOriginal: Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future
items.description: Αυτή η ιστορία έχει εκδοθεί από κοινού από το Reasons to be Cheerful και το Outrider Foundation . Το 2012, ο Philip Wallisfurth ήθελε να σώσει ένα δέντρο. Πολίτες στο Άαχεν της Γερμανίας διαμαρτυρήθηκαν για τα σχέδια για ένα εμπορικό κέντρο που απειλούσε ένα δέντρο 150 ετών. Ο Wallisfurth, τότε ένας επίδοξος καλλιτέχνης του δρόμου, αναρωτήθηκε αν μπορούσε να χρησιμοποιήσει βρύα - αντί για τα συνηθισμένα του…
items.descriptionOriginal: This story has been co-published by Reasons to be Cheerful and the Outrider Foundation . I n 2012, Philip Wallisfurth wanted to save a tree. Citizens in Aachen, Germany, were protesting plans for a shopping center that threatened a 150-year-old tree. Wallisfurth , then an aspiring street artist, wondered if he could use moss — instead of his usual spray can — to support the campaign. He harvested moss from a local park, used yogurt as an adhesive and stuck two-meter-high letters onto the construction fence, spelling out “greener living.” The reactions surprised him. “People loved it,” he recalls. “Many took pictures and some spontaneously hung flowers in small vases onto the fence.” He had stumbled upon a medium that was soft, tactile and alive — and a natural way of occupying public space. YouTube tutorials suggested mixing moss with buttermilk in a blender, but the results disappointed him. Through trial and error with different mosses and yogurts, he developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti.” Artist Philip Wallisfurth developed his own approach to making “bio-graffiti with moss.” Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth Two years later, whiskey maker Jack Daniel’s hired him for a campaign. In Cologne, Wallisfurth covered an eight-by-eight-meter wall with moss lettering, spelling out a motto he lives by: never give up trying to do what you really want to be happy Now an artist with international projects and a studio in Berlin, Wallisfurth, 42, mostly paints large, colorful murals and designs anamorphic installations, room-filling works that seem to change shape depending on the viewer’s perspective. But moss continues to appeal to him for several reasons. He feels it’s uniquely suited to transform uninspiring urban spaces into places that feel more welcoming — and it has environmental benefits, too. He learned from speaking with scientists that moss can convert carbon monoxide and nitrogen dioxide into oxygen. “It also acts as a natural air filter and absorbs noise,” he notes. Moss continues to appeal to Wallisfurth for its ability to make spaces more welcoming and its environmental benefits. Courtesy of Philip Wallisfurth There are more than 13,000 recognized species of moss. The unassuming plant that most homeowners would like to scrape off their driveways offers more than unusual shades of green. It can retain moisture, dampen sound and, under the right conditions, help regulate the temperature of the surfaces it covers. Wallisfurth dreams of turning entire structures — for instance, train stations — into buildings where moss improves the air and atmosphere. As cities grapple with increasingly dangerous heat, Wallisfurth’s artistic experiments intersect with a serious question for architects and climate researchers: While concrete, asphalt and masonry store the sun’s energy, cities are searching for ways to keep buildings and public spaces cooler. Could this small, overlooked plant become part of the answer? Weighed down by negative news? Enter your email below to receive our smart, uplifting newsletters. Or click here to choose exactly which ones you want [contact-form-7] Moss is remarkably adaptable. It has no conventional root system but absorbs moisture directly through its surface and can tolerate long periods of dehydration. A 2026 field study in Seoul showed moss-based green roofs reduced peak roof-surface temperatures by about 19° Celsius and maximum indoor temperatures by 2 to 3.5° Celsius during heat waves, while a 2026 peer-reviewed study from TU Delft in the Netherlands found that hydrated moss can produce evaporative cooling and insulate underlying surfaces. Credit: Lukas Gojda / Shutterstock Moss is remarkably adaptable. It has no conventional root system but absorbs moisture directly through its surface and can tolerate long periods of dehydration. It can retain moisture, dampen sound and, under the right conditions, help regulate the temperature of the surfaces it covers. As promising as these findings are, the reality is more complex than a green coating that simply cools whatever it covers. According to the Dutch researchers, the cooling effect only lasts as long as the moss is hydrated. Crucially, they found that dry moss exposed to direct sun can actually become warmer than bare mortar. So the question changes: Can cities engineer walls and roofs with moss that stays moist when cities most need cooling? Several startups are betting that the solution lies in redesigning the surfaces themselves. In London, Alive Labs produces moss-covered panels to turn city walls into living infrastructure. Founder and architect Nicky Naidu wants to change how the construction industry thinks about moss, which is often treated as a sign of neglect. “Moss gets a bad rep. But moss has intrinsic beauty, and we want to bring that beauty to cities,” Naidu told Reuters . “It’s carbon negative, bioreceptive, cost-effective and fire-safe. Everything that the industry needs and requires.” The company’s panels are made of a base material Naidu describes as bioreceptive concrete designed to support the growth of moss. The living wall systems incorporate controlled irrigation, delivering moisture directly rather than relying on rainfall or conventional surface spraying. Naidu argues that the moss walls are easier to maintain than conventional green walls because moss needs no soil to flourish. Alive Labs produces moss-covered panels to turn city walls into living infrastructure. Courtesy of Alive Labs In the Netherlands, Respyre has developed a similar concept with “Mosscrete,” a bioreceptive concrete that can be seeded with moss and also features an “ integrated, automated irrigation system that keeps the moss sufficiently hydrated, particularly during warmer and drier periods .” Both companies have moved from the prototype stage to making their panels commercially available. In Berlin, Green City Solutions built the world’s first vertical moss farm on 1,200 square meters to grow moss for sustainable air filters. The next step for the industry is to measure results in real life under varying temperatures and conditions, to determine where moss performs well enough to justify the investment. Not every experiment requires new materials or elaborate infrastructure. In Santiago de Compostela, Spain, a chance observation during the pandemic led city officials and university researchers to reconsider the vegetation growing between the city’s paving stones, including moss. After thermal cameras showed that stone surfaces with these small patches of greenery measured up to 25° Celsius cooler than bare paving, the city opted to leave the “urban microgreen” in place as a low-cost way to mitigate heat. A Respyre test panel after irrigation. Courtesy of Respyre Philip Wallisfurth keeps experimenting with the greenery, too. For a temporary installation, he transformed an entire living room in Berlin into an otherworldly moss-covered landscape. Again, he noticed people’s positive reaction. “The smell simply calmed people down,” he observed. “If you had a living moss wall in an office that was regularly watered, it would create an incredibly pleasant working climate. Plus, it filters the air and absorbs noise — it’s actually dreamlike.” Wallisfurth learned that most conventional moss art one finds in rooms is made from moss that has been dried and preserved with chemicals, eliminating the need to water it but also killing most of its environmental benefits. “It’s dead,” he says. His own bio-art has limits. Without preservation, the moss typically dries and dies within three to six months, depending on the surrounding dryness and acidity. “Like street art,” Wallisfurth notes, “it’s impermanent, too.” The walls of a bank building in Utrecht before and after renovation with Respyre’s bioreceptive concrete. Courtesy of Respyre But learning more about moss also made him reconsider where his material comes from. His sister, a nature guide, calls moss the “lungs of the forest” and told him it was wrong to take moss from forests and public spaces. He now sources his moss from an abandoned army training ground that is likely to soon be a construction site. His desire to create sustainable moss installations sometimes clashes with his clients’ expectations. Several big corporations approached him about creating moss pieces, he says, only to dismiss his concerns about sustainable sourcing. “They told me: ‘We don’t care. It just needs to look green in the pictures.’” He shakes his head. “That was a downer. It showed that most people only look at it as a means to an end.” The exchange captures a broader risk in the rush to make cities greener: The living material can become a visual shorthand for sustainability, even when its environmental value has not been proven. It might look green but actually be greenwashing. Credit: CinemaPhoto / Shutterstock “If you had a living moss wall in an office that was regularly watered, it would create an incredibly pleasant working climate. Plus, it filters the air and absorbs noise — it’s actually dreamlike.” –Philip Wallisfurth In addition to making his own moss art, Wallisfurth enjoys running moss workshops for kids at schools. Children love to experiment with the soft, tactile material, he says. Growing up in a rural part of the Eifel in Germany, he remembers walking barefoot across moss, and nature was his refuge when his own childhood was marked by loss. His parents died of cancer when he was young, and his brother was killed when Wallisfurth was only 14. He trained as a foreign-language correspondent and hotel manager before moving to Berlin and pursuing art. He turned to art explicitly as a means to brighten places up and turn rooms into positive spaces. “That’s what drives me,” he says. “Positivity is simply a much better way to deal with things. Of course, not everything is positive, but I have to try to stay positive.” His favorite projects begin with dark, inhospitable places and turn them into areas where people like to spend time. “That’s my goal as an artist.” Wait, you're not a member yet? Join the Reasons to be Cheerful community by supporting our nonprofit publication and giving what you can. Join Cancel anytime He believes he wouldn’t be an artist without his biography. And he sees a similar resilience in the plants: “A specialist once told me I could put moss in the oven at 270° Celsius, and if I water it afterward, it will come back to life.” In that way, he says, “Maybe I’m a little like moss. You can destroy it, but it simply grows again. It’s a fighter.” The post Imagining the Mossy Cities of the Future appeared first on Reasons to be Cheerful .

items.description: Τριάντα χρόνια αφότου η μητέρα της πέθανε ξαφνικά ενώ υπηρετούσε στο Ειρηνευτικό Σώμα, η Κέιτ Ρόγκαν εξακολουθεί να κουβαλά τη μνήμη ενός ξένου που συνάντησε τη θλίψη της με τέσσερις ήσυχες λέξεις: «Έλα μαζί μου. Σε πήρα». Η γυναίκα καθοδήγησε τον Ρόγκαν από ένα προσγειωμένο αεροπλάνο, μέσω μιας πτήσης που ακυρώθηκε, σε μια νύχτα ξενοδοχείου και μέχρι την αγκαλιά της αδερφής της στο baggage cla…
items.descriptionOriginal: Thirty years after her mother died suddenly while she was serving in the Peace Corps, Kate Rogan still carries the memory of a stranger who met her grief with four quiet words: "Come with me. I got you." The woman guided Rogan off a grounded plane, through a canceled flight, through a hotel night, and all the way to her sister's arms at baggage claim - then disappeared, nameless, into ordinary life. What stays is not just the kindness, but what Rogan came to understand about herself in that moment: "I was this strong, independent young woman, but in that moment, I could not handle life without somebody helping me." Some losses crack us open in ways that expose how much we need each other, and some strangers seem to know this before we do.
